content.purpose: Screen for adult ADHD and assess symptom patterns across inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity domains.

items.text: How often do you have trouble wrapping up the final details of a project, once the challenging parts have been done?
How often do you have difficulty getting things in order when you have to do a task that requires organization?
How often do you have problems remembering appointments or obligations?
When you have a task that requires a lot of thought, how often do you avoid or delay getting started?
How often do you fidget or squirm with your hands or feet when you have to sit down for a long time?
How often do you feel overly active and compelled to do things, like you were driven by a motor?
How often do you make careless mistakes when you have to work on a boring or difficult project?
How often do you have difficulty keeping your attention when you are doing boring or repetitive work?
How often do you have difficulty concentrating on what people say to you, even when they are speaking to you directly?
How often do you misplace or have difficulty finding things at home or at work?
How often are you distracted by activity or noise around you?
How often do you leave your seat in meetings or other situations in which you are expected to remain seated?
How often do you feel restless or fidgety?
How often do you have difficulty unwinding and relaxing when you have time to yourself?
How often do you find yourself talking too much when you are in social situations?
When you're in a conversation, how often do you find yourself finishing the sentences of the people you are talking to, before they can finish them themselves?
How often do you have difficulty waiting your turn in situations when turn taking is required?
How often do you interrupt others when they are busy?

clinical_interpretations.Low: Your scores indicate minimal ADHD symptoms. Part A score ≤9 and total score ≤30 are both below clinical thresholds, consistent with typical adult functioning without clinically significant ADHD symptoms.
clinical_interpretations.Mild to Moderate: Your scores are in the mild to moderate range. If Part A is 10-13 (below diagnostic threshold) but total score approaches 40+ (79th percentile), clinical evaluation may still be warranted as this pattern can be diagnostically informative.
clinical_interpretations.High: Your scores indicate clinically significant ADHD symptoms. Part A scores 14-17 meet the diagnostic threshold, and/or total scores 40-49 exceed the 79th percentile where most individuals with ADHD score. Professional evaluation is recommended.
clinical_interpretations.Very High: Your scores indicate severe ADHD symptoms. Part A scores ≥18 or total scores ≥50 represent very high symptom levels that are strongly consistent with ADHD diagnosis and require comprehensive clinical evaluation.

sections.title: About the ASSIST v3.0
sections.text: The WHO Alcohol, Smoking and Substance Involvement Screening Test (ASSIST) v3.0 is a validated screening instrument that identifies substance use risk across 10 categories. It provides specific risk levels and intervention recommendations based on standardized WHO criteria and has been validated in multiple countries and healthcare settings.

sections.title: Instructions
sections.text: Please answer each question honestly based on your substance use experiences. For prescription medications, only consider non-medical use (taking more than prescribed, using without a prescription, or using for non-medical reasons). All responses are confidential and will help determine appropriate next steps for your health and wellbeing.

sections.title: Scoring and Interpretation
sections.text: The ASSIST calculates separate involvement scores for each substance category by adding scores from questions 2-7 (excluding tobacco question 5). Risk levels are determined by specific thresholds: tobacco and illicit substances use 0-3/4-26/27+ thresholds, while alcohol uses 0-10/11-26/27+ thresholds reflecting its legal status and different risk profile.

severe_anxiety.message: Severe anxiety - may require clinical intervention

clinical_interpretations.Minimal: Your score suggests minimal anxiety symptoms. This is within the normal range. Continue monitoring your mental health and maintain healthy coping strategies such as regular exercise, adequate sleep, and stress management techniques.
clinical_interpretations.Mild: Your score indicates mild anxiety symptoms that may occasionally interfere with daily activities. Consider lifestyle modifications including regular physical activity, mindfulness practices, limiting caffeine intake, and ensuring adequate sleep. If symptoms persist or worsen over several weeks, consider consulting a healthcare professional.
clinical_interpretations.Moderate: Your score suggests moderate anxiety symptoms that are likely interfering with your daily activities and quality of life. Treatment options may include counseling, therapy (such as cognitive-behavioral therapy), lifestyle modifications, or other evidence-based interventions.
clinical_interpretations.Severe: Your score indicates severe anxiety symptoms that are significantly impacting your daily functioning and well-being. It is important to consult with a healthcare professional promptly for comprehensive evaluation and treatment planning. Severe anxiety is highly treatable with appropriate professional care, which may include therapy, medication, or a combination of treatments.

sections.title: About the GAD-7
sections.text: The Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) is a brief self-report tool designed to screen for generalized anxiety disorder and assess its severity. It is based on DSM-IV criteria for GAD and is also useful for identifying other anxiety disorders.

sections.title: Instructions
sections.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by the following problems? For each item, select the response that best describes your experience.

sections.title: Scoring and Interpretation
sections.text: Add up all checked boxes for a total score. Anxiety severity bands: 0–4 minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–21 severe anxiety.

sections.title: Clinical Applications
sections.text: The GAD-7 is widely used in primary care, mental health, and research settings. It can be used for initial screening, monitoring treatment progress, and assessing outcomes for anxiety disorders.

sections.title: About the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
sections.text: The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is a national network of local crisis centers that provides free and confidential emotional support to people in suicidal crisis or emotional distress 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, across the United States. In July 2022, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline transitioned to the easy-to-remember 988 dialing code. The Lifeline is funded by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) and is operated by Vibrant Emotional Health.

sections.title: Who Should Reach Out
sections.text: The 988 Lifeline is for anyone experiencing thoughts of suicide, mental health crisis, or emotional distress. You don't have to be suicidal to call. People contact 988 for many reasons including overwhelming anxiety, depression, relationship problems, loneliness, substance use concerns, grief, or simply needing someone to talk to. The service also supports family members and friends who are worried about a loved one.

sections.title: How to Reach the Lifeline
sections.text: You can reach the 988 Lifeline by calling or texting 988 from any phone in the United States. Online chat is available at 988lifeline.org/chat. For veterans and service members, press 1 after dialing 988 to reach the Veterans Crisis Line. Spanish-speaking counselors are available by pressing 2. TTY users can dial 711 then 988. All services are free and confidential.

sections.title: What to Expect When You Contact 988
sections.text: When you call, text, or chat 988, you'll be connected with a trained crisis counselor at a local crisis center. The counselor will listen without judgment, help you explore your feelings, discuss coping strategies, and connect you with local resources if needed. Conversations are confidential unless there is imminent danger to life. Average wait times vary but are typically under 5 minutes. You can stay on the line as long as you need.

sections.title: Specialized Services
sections.text: The 988 Lifeline offers specialized support including the Veterans Crisis Line (press 1), Spanish-language services (press 2), and the LGBTQ+ Lifeline which provides crisis support for LGBTQ+ young people. Native and Indigenous people can connect with counselors familiar with Native cultures. The Lifeline also offers resources for loss survivors, attempt survivors, and people supporting someone in crisis.

sections.title: About AASRA
sections.text: AASRA is one of India's most recognized suicide prevention and mental health helplines, providing crisis support to people across the country. Founded in Mumbai, AASRA offers a listening ear to anyone experiencing suicidal thoughts, depression, anxiety, or emotional distress. The organization works to prevent suicide through crisis intervention, raising awareness about mental health, and training volunteers to provide compassionate support. AASRA has been serving the Indian community for many years and continues to be a vital resource for those in need.

sections.title: Crisis Counseling
sections.text: AASRA's trained volunteers provide crisis counseling and emotional support via phone. When you call, a volunteer will listen without judgment and help you through your difficult moment. Services are available in Hindi and English. AASRA also provides follow-up support and can connect callers with additional mental health resources.

sections.title: Who Should Call
sections.text: Anyone in India experiencing suicidal thoughts, severe depression, anxiety, or emotional crisis can call AASRA. The service also supports those dealing with grief, relationship problems, loneliness, and other life challenges. Family members concerned about a loved one can call for guidance on how to help.

sections.title: How to Get Help
sections.text: Call AASRA at 91-9820466726 for crisis support. The service is available 24/7. Visit aasra.info for additional resources about suicide prevention and mental health. For international crisis resources, visit Befrienders Worldwide at befrienders.org.

sections.title: About ANAD
sections.text: The National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders (ANAD) is one of the oldest nonprofit organizations dedicated to eating disorder awareness, prevention, and recovery support. Founded in 1976, ANAD provides free peer support services, educational resources, and advocacy for individuals affected by eating disorders and their families. ANAD believes that recovery is possible and works to provide hope and support to those on the journey to healing.

sections.title: ANAD Helpline
sections.text: ANAD's Helpline at 1-888-375-7767 provides free support, information, and referrals for anyone affected by an eating disorder. Helpline staff can help you understand eating disorders, find treatment providers, locate support groups, and navigate recovery challenges. The helpline serves individuals with eating disorders, concerned family members and friends, and professionals seeking resources. Staff provide compassionate, non-judgmental support and can help you take the next step toward recovery.

sections.title: Free Support Groups
sections.text: ANAD operates free support groups for individuals in recovery from eating disorders and for their loved ones. Support groups meet virtually, making them accessible from anywhere. Groups are led by trained facilitators who have personal experience with eating disorder recovery. In these groups, members share their experiences, struggles, and victories in a confidential, supportive environment. Specialized groups are available for different stages of recovery and for specific populations including teens, men, and parents.

sections.title: Understanding Eating Disorders
sections.text: ANAD provides education about all types of eating disorders including anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, ARFID, and other specified feeding and eating disorders. Educational resources cover warning signs, health consequences, treatment options, and recovery processes. ANAD emphasizes that eating disorders are serious mental illnesses that affect people of all genders, ages, races, and body sizes. Early intervention improves outcomes, and recovery is possible at any stage.

sections.title: Recovery Resources
sections.text: Beyond the helpline and support groups, ANAD offers a treatment directory to help individuals and families find eating disorder specialists. The website provides recovery tools, meal support resources, and educational materials for various stages of the recovery journey. ANAD's Recovery Mentorship Program connects those in recovery with mentors who have successfully navigated their own recovery. The organization also provides resources for educators, coaches, and healthcare providers on recognizing and responding to eating disorders.

sections.title: About Befrienders Worldwide
sections.text: Befrienders Worldwide is an international organization connecting people in emotional distress with crisis support services around the globe. Founded in 1974, Befrienders Worldwide coordinates a network of emotional support centers in over 30 countries across Africa, the Americas, Asia, Australia, Europe, and the Middle East. The organization provides a vital directory service helping people anywhere in the world find local crisis support in their language and time zone.

sections.title: Finding Help Worldwide
sections.text: The Befrienders Worldwide website maintains a directory of crisis support services organized by country and region. Each listing includes contact information, hours of operation, and available services. Whether you're in Argentina, Bangladesh, Japan, Nigeria, Sweden, or anywhere else, the directory can help you find local support. This makes Befrienders Worldwide an essential resource for travelers, expatriates, or anyone seeking help in a country other than their home.

sections.title: Emotional Support Services
sections.text: Member centers provide emotional support to anyone in distress, not only those who are suicidal. Common reasons people reach out include loneliness, depression, anxiety, relationship problems, grief, and life crises. Befrienders centers use a listening approach—trained volunteers provide a non-judgmental, confidential space for people to express their feelings and be heard. This simple act of listening can be powerful for people who feel alone in their struggles.

sections.title: Global Volunteer Network
sections.text: Befrienders centers are typically staffed by trained volunteers who provide emotional support through phone, email, or in-person visits depending on the center. Volunteers receive training in active listening, confidentiality, and supporting people in distress. The volunteer model ensures that support is available even in regions with limited mental health professional resources. Befrienders Worldwide provides training resources and standards to maintain quality across its global network.

sections.title: How to Use Befrienders Worldwide
sections.text: Visit befrienders.org and click on your region to find crisis support services in your country. Each listing provides contact details and information about available services. If you cannot find a service in your country, the website provides guidance on other international resources. Befrienders Worldwide also offers email support directly for people who cannot reach local services. Remember that services vary by location, so check individual center details for hours and contact methods.

sections.title: About BlackLine
sections.text: BlackLine provides a space for peer support, counseling, and resource sharing for people who are Black, BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, People of Color), and LGBTQ+. Unlike traditional crisis lines, BlackLine centers the experiences of marginalized communities and provides culturally-responsive support from counselors who share similar lived experiences. The organization recognizes that mainstream crisis services may not feel safe or culturally appropriate for everyone, and offers an alternative rooted in community care and cultural understanding.

sections.title: Who BlackLine Serves
sections.text: BlackLine serves Black people, Indigenous people, people of color, and LGBTQ+ individuals who are experiencing distress, crisis, or simply need someone to talk to who understands their experience. You can call when you're experiencing emotional crisis, dealing with racism or discrimination, facing challenges related to your identity, or need support navigating systems. BlackLine is especially valuable for those who want to speak with someone who understands the unique stressors and historical traumas that affect Black, Brown, and Indigenous communities.

sections.title: How to Reach BlackLine
sections.text: Call 1-800-604-5841 to speak with a peer counselor. Check the website at callblackline.com for current hours of operation, as hours may vary. When you call, you'll be connected with a trained counselor who can provide emotional support, crisis intervention, and connections to resources. BlackLine prioritizes hiring Black, BIPOC, and LGBTQ+ counselors who can provide culturally-competent support and understand the intersectional experiences of callers.

sections.title: What BlackLine Offers
sections.text: BlackLine provides peer support and emotional counseling that acknowledges the impact of systemic racism, historical trauma, and discrimination on mental health. Counselors can help with crisis support, emotional processing, safety planning, and connecting to community resources. The line offers a space to talk through experiences with racism, anti-Black violence, homophobia, transphobia, and other forms of oppression without having to explain or educate. BlackLine approaches support from a framework of community care rather than clinical intervention.

sections.title: Community-Centered Support
sections.text: BlackLine operates from principles of community care, recognizing that healing happens in connection with others who share similar experiences. The organization focuses on building power and resilience within Black, BIPOC, and LGBTQ+ communities. This approach acknowledges that for many marginalized people, standard crisis intervention approaches may not address the root causes of distress—systemic oppression, racism, poverty, and discrimination. BlackLine aims to provide support that affirms identities and empowers callers rather than pathologizing their responses to oppressive circumstances.

content.name: Boys Town National Hotline
content.summary: 24/7 crisis support for youth and parents facing family problems, bullying, suicide, and more.

sections.title: About the Boys Town National Hotline
sections.text: The Boys Town National Hotline is a 24-hour crisis, resource, and referral line for children, teens, and parents facing various issues including family problems, bullying, abuse, suicide, and more. Run by Boys Town—a nonprofit organization founded in 1917 to help at-risk youth—the hotline provides free, confidential support from trained counselors who specialize in helping young people and families. The hotline has helped millions of callers since its founding and serves youth and families across the United States.

sections.title: Who the Hotline Serves
sections.text: The hotline serves both youth and parents. Young people can call about problems with parents, school stress, bullying, depression, abuse, running away, suicidal thoughts, substance use, relationships, and more. Parents can call for help with parenting challenges, communication issues, concerns about their child's behavior or mental health, and guidance on getting help for their family. There's no problem too big or too small—if you're struggling, the hotline is here to help.

sections.title: How to Reach the Hotline
sections.text: Call 1-800-448-3000 any time, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Text VOICE to 20121 to reach a crisis counselor via text. Spanish-speaking counselors are available. All calls are free and confidential. When you call, you'll speak with a trained Boys Town counselor who will listen to your concerns, help you work through the situation, and connect you with local resources if needed. There's no cost and no judgment.

sections.title: What Counselors Provide
sections.text: Boys Town counselors are trained in crisis intervention and can help with a wide range of issues affecting youth and families. Counselors provide emotional support, help callers work through problems and develop solutions, offer information about community resources, and can connect families with local services when needed. For youth in crisis, counselors can help create safety plans and provide ongoing support. Counselors use Boys Town's evidence-based model focused on building healthy relationships and communication skills.

sections.title: Boys Town Resources
sections.text: Beyond the hotline, Boys Town offers extensive resources for families including parenting tips and guides on the Boys Town website, a free parenting app, and information about Boys Town's residential and community programs for at-risk youth. Boys Town's parenting advice is based on decades of research and practice with children and families. The organization also offers direct care programs for youth who need more intensive support, including residential care, in-home family services, and school-based programs.

content.name: Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline
content.summary: 24/7 professional crisis counseling for child abuse, neglect, and other family issues.

sections.title: About the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline
sections.text: The Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline is a 24-hour hotline dedicated to the prevention of child abuse and serving children and adults who have been victims of abuse or neglect. Operated by Childhelp, one of the nation's leading organizations for child abuse prevention and treatment, the hotline provides crisis intervention, information, and referrals to emergency, social service, and support resources. Professional crisis counselors answer calls around the clock, providing immediate support and guidance.

sections.title: Who Can Call the Hotline
sections.text: Anyone can call—children who are being abused or neglected, adult survivors of childhood abuse, parents who need help or are struggling with parenting challenges, concerned family members, neighbors, or teachers who suspect a child is being abused, and professionals seeking information or resources. The hotline serves people in crisis as well as those seeking information about child abuse prevention, reporting requirements, or local resources.

sections.title: How to Reach the Hotline
sections.text: Call 1-800-4-A-CHILD (1-800-422-4453) any time, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. The hotline is staffed by professional crisis counselors who can provide immediate support and connect callers with local resources. Services are available in English and Spanish, with access to interpreters in over 170 languages. All calls are confidential. The hotline does not directly report abuse but can provide guidance on how to make a report in your area if needed.

sections.title: What the Hotline Provides
sections.text: Hotline counselors provide crisis intervention for children and adults in immediate distress, information about child abuse signs, reporting procedures, and prevention, emotional support for survivors of childhood abuse, guidance for parents struggling with parenting challenges, referrals to local child protective services, counseling services, and support groups, and resources for professionals working with children and families. Counselors help callers understand their options and take next steps.

sections.title: About Childhelp
sections.text: Childhelp is a national nonprofit organization dedicated to helping victims of child abuse and neglect. Founded in 1959, Childhelp operates the National Child Abuse Hotline, residential treatment facilities for severely abused children, child advocacy centers, foster care, and adoption programs. The organization's mission is to meet the physical, emotional, educational, and spiritual needs of abused, neglected, and at-risk children. Childhelp also works on prevention through education programs and advocacy for child protection laws.

content.name: Crisis Text Line
content.description: Free 24/7 support via text. Text HOME to 741741 to connect with a trained crisis counselor for any type of crisis situation.
content.summary: Free 24/7 support via text. Text HOME to 741741 for crisis counseling.

sections.title: About Crisis Text Line
sections.text: Crisis Text Line is a free, 24/7 text-based mental health support service that connects people in crisis with trained crisis counselors. Founded in 2013, Crisis Text Line has become one of the largest crisis intervention services in the United States, processing millions of text conversations with people experiencing emotional distress, anxiety, depression, suicidal thoughts, relationship issues, and other challenges.

sections.title: Who Should Text
sections.text: Crisis Text Line is for anyone struggling with any type of crisis, not just suicide. Common reasons people text include anxiety, depression, stress, self-harm, bullying, relationship problems, eating disorders, grief, loneliness, and substance use. The service is especially popular among young people who may prefer texting over calling. You don't need to be in immediate danger to reach out—the service supports anyone who needs help.

sections.title: How to Reach Crisis Text Line
sections.text: Text HOME to 741741 from anywhere in the United States. You can also text from Canada (text HOME to 686868), UK (text HELLO to 85258), or Ireland (text HELLO to 50808). The service is completely free—standard text messaging rates may apply depending on your phone plan. Conversations are confidential and secure.

sections.title: What to Expect When You Text
sections.text: When you text HOME to 741741, you'll receive an automated response while being connected to a live, trained crisis counselor. The counselor will introduce themselves and ask how they can help. They'll listen, provide emotional support, and help you work through your feelings using evidence-based techniques. Conversations typically last 15-45 minutes but can go longer if needed. You can end the conversation at any time.

sections.title: About Crisis Counselors
sections.text: Crisis Text Line counselors are trained volunteers who complete a rigorous 30-hour training program and ongoing education. They are supervised by licensed clinical professionals during every shift. Counselors use collaborative problem-solving and active listening techniques to help texters move from a hot moment to a cool calm. The service uses data and technology to improve crisis intervention while maintaining strict privacy standards.

sections.title: Privacy and Safety
sections.text: Crisis Text Line takes privacy seriously. Conversations are encrypted and confidential. The organization maintains strict data protection policies and does not share personal information with third parties without consent. In rare cases where there is immediate danger to life, Crisis Text Line may contact emergency services—but this happens in less than 1% of conversations. The service is designed to be discreet, making it easier for people in sensitive situations to reach out for help without others knowing.

sections.title: Beyond the Text Line
sections.text: After your conversation, Crisis Text Line can connect you with local resources, ongoing mental health services, and additional support. The organization's website offers self-help resources, information about mental health conditions, and guidance for supporting loved ones in crisis. Crisis Text Line also partners with schools, workplaces, and organizations to bring crisis support to more communities. The service has answered millions of text conversations and continues to expand its reach to help more people in need.

content.name: DeafLEAD Hotline

content.description: DeafLEAD provides crisis intervention and mental health support services specifically designed for deaf, hard of hearing, and DeafBlind individuals using ASL and videophone technology.

sections.title: About DeafLEAD
sections.text: DeafLEAD is a nonprofit organization that provides crisis intervention, mental health support, and advocacy services specifically for deaf, hard of hearing, and DeafBlind individuals. Understanding that traditional crisis services are often inaccessible to the deaf community, DeafLEAD offers services in American Sign Language through videophone technology, ensuring that deaf individuals can receive support in their native language from counselors who understand deaf culture and experiences.

sections.title: Crisis Services
sections.text: DeafLEAD's crisis intervention services are available via videophone, allowing deaf individuals to communicate in ASL with trained crisis counselors. Services address a range of issues including suicidal thoughts, domestic violence, sexual assault, and general emotional distress. Counselors are trained in both crisis intervention and deaf culture, providing culturally competent support that respects the unique experiences and communication needs of deaf individuals.

sections.title: Accessible Support
sections.text: Unlike mainstream crisis services that may only offer TTY or relay services, DeafLEAD provides direct ASL communication through videophone, eliminating the barriers of text-based communication. For DeafBlind individuals, specialized accommodations are available. This accessibility ensures that deaf individuals in crisis can receive immediate, effective support without the delays and miscommunication that often occur when using interpreters or text-based services.

sections.title: How to Get Help
sections.text: To access DeafLEAD's crisis services, visit their website to find current videophone numbers and hours. If you are a deaf, hard of hearing, or DeafBlind individual experiencing a mental health crisis, domestic violence, or other emergency, DeafLEAD's trained counselors can provide support in ASL. Services are confidential and designed specifically for your community's communication needs.

content.name: Disaster Distress Helpline
content.summary: 24/7 crisis counseling and support for people experiencing emotional distress related to disasters.

sections.title: About the Disaster Distress Helpline
sections.text: The Disaster Distress Helpline (DDH) provides 24/7, 365-day-a-year crisis counseling and support to people experiencing emotional distress related to natural or human-caused disasters. Operated by SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration), the helpline provides immediate crisis counseling by trained counselors who understand the unique psychological impacts of disasters. The service is free, multilingual, and confidential, serving as a vital resource during times of crisis.

sections.title: Who Should Contact the Helpline
sections.text: Anyone experiencing emotional distress related to a disaster can call—whether you've been directly affected, are a first responder, or are struggling while watching events unfold in the news. Disasters include hurricanes, floods, wildfires, earthquakes, tornadoes, pandemics, mass violence incidents, oil spills, and other traumatic events. You don't need to be in the immediate disaster area; watching repeated news coverage of disasters can also cause significant distress. The helpline also serves people who were impacted by past disasters and are experiencing recurring emotional difficulties.

sections.title: How to Reach the Helpline
sections.text: Call 1-800-985-5990 any time, 24/7, to speak with a trained crisis counselor. Text TalkWithUs to 66746 for text-based support. Spanish speakers can call and press 2 for Spanish, or text HABLANOS to 66746. The helpline is staffed by trained counselors from a network of crisis centers across the country. For callers who are deaf or hard of hearing, TTY services are available at 1-800-846-8517. Services are available in over 100 languages through translation services.

sections.title: What Happens When You Call
sections.text: When you contact the Disaster Distress Helpline, a trained crisis counselor will listen to your concerns and provide emotional support, coping strategies, and information. Counselors can help you understand normal reactions to disasters, develop a plan for managing stress, and connect you with local resources and support services. Calls are confidential, and you can remain anonymous. The helpline does not provide physical aid or financial assistance but can connect you with organizations that do.

sections.title: Disaster Behavioral Health Resources
sections.text: Beyond the helpline, SAMHSA provides extensive resources for coping with disasters including tip sheets, fact sheets, and guides for specific populations such as children, older adults, and first responders. The Disaster Behavioral Health Information Series addresses topics like coping with grief after a disaster, helping children cope, and recognizing signs of trauma. SAMHSA also supports Crisis Counseling Programs in federally declared disaster areas, providing free counseling and support services to affected communities.

org.name: SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration)

content.name: LGBT National Help Center
content.summary: Peer support and local resources for LGBTQ+ individuals through phone and online chat.

sections.title: About the LGBT National Help Center
sections.text: The LGBT National Help Center provides free and confidential peer support and local resources for LGBTQ+ individuals, their families, and allies. Operating since 1996, the Help Center runs three specialized phone lines and online chat services staffed by trained volunteers from the LGBTQ+ community. The organization serves people of all ages who are looking for a safe space to talk about their identity, struggles, coming out process, or any issues related to being LGBTQ+.

sections.title: Phone Lines and Services
sections.text: The LGBT National Hotline (1-888-843-4564) serves all ages and provides peer support, information, and local resources. The LGBT National Youth Talkline (1-800-246-7743) specifically serves youth ages 25 and under with peer support from young volunteers who understand the unique challenges LGBTQ+ youth face. The LGBT National Senior Hotline (1-888-234-7243) provides support for LGBTQ+ seniors who may face isolation and unique challenges. All lines connect callers with trained peer volunteers.

sections.title: Who Contacts the Help Center
sections.text: People contact the Help Center for many reasons: questioning their sexual orientation or gender identity, preparing to come out, dealing with family rejection or acceptance, navigating relationships, experiencing discrimination or harassment, feeling isolated or alone, seeking LGBTQ+-friendly resources in their area, or simply wanting to talk to someone who understands. Parents and family members also call seeking support and information to help them understand and support LGBTQ+ loved ones.

sections.title: How to Reach the Help Center
sections.text: Call the main Hotline at 1-888-843-4564, the Youth Talkline at 1-800-246-7743, or the Senior Hotline at 1-888-234-7243. Check the website for current hours as they vary by day. Online chat is available through lgbthotline.org. All services are free and confidential. Volunteers can provide peer support, information about LGBTQ+ topics, and connections to local resources including support groups, community centers, and LGBTQ+-affirming service providers.

sections.title: Peer Support Approach
sections.text: The LGBT National Help Center uses a peer support model, meaning volunteers are members of the LGBTQ+ community who have been trained to provide compassionate, non-judgmental support. Peer volunteers understand firsthand the experiences and challenges of being LGBTQ+ in today's world. This shared experience creates a unique connection and helps callers feel truly understood. Volunteers listen, provide information, and help callers explore their feelings and options without pushing any particular path.

content.name: Lifeline Australia
content.summary: National crisis support and suicide prevention line for anyone in Australia.

sections.title: About Lifeline Australia
sections.text: Lifeline Australia is a national charity providing all Australians experiencing emotional distress with access to 24-hour crisis support and suicide prevention services. Since its founding in 1963 by Methodist minister Reverend Sir Alan Walker, Lifeline has become one of Australia's most trusted crisis support organizations. The service operates on the belief that no person should have to face their darkest moments alone. Lifeline's vision is an Australia free of suicide, and the organization works toward this through direct support, community education, and advocacy.

sections.title: Who Should Contact Lifeline
sections.text: Lifeline is available to any Australian experiencing a personal crisis or thinking about suicide. You can call if you're feeling overwhelmed, anxious, depressed, lonely, or are going through a difficult life event. Lifeline also supports people worried about a friend or family member. You don't need to be in immediate crisis—Lifeline helps people at all stages of distress, from those needing someone to talk to through to those experiencing suicidal thoughts. The service is free, confidential, and available to people of all ages and backgrounds.

sections.title: How to Reach Lifeline
sections.text: Call 13 11 14 any time, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Calls are answered by trained Crisis Supporters from Lifeline centres across Australia. For text-based support, you can also contact Lifeline via text on 0477 13 11 14 (available 6pm-midnight AEDT) or chat online at lifeline.org.au. Video chat support is available for Deaf and hard of hearing individuals through the National Relay Service. Service is provided in English with interpreter services available.

sections.title: What Happens When You Contact Lifeline
sections.text: When you contact Lifeline, you'll be connected with a trained Crisis Supporter who will listen without judgment. Crisis Supporters are trained to provide emotional support, help you explore your options, and assist with safety planning if needed. Your call is confidential—Lifeline will only contact emergency services if there is serious concern for your safety or the safety of others. You can remain anonymous, and your call will not appear identified on phone bills. There's no time limit on calls, and you can reach out as often as you need.

sections.title: Additional Lifeline Services
sections.text: Beyond crisis support, Lifeline offers DV-alert (domestic and family violence training for frontline workers), Eclipse (support for young people affected by suicide), and community-based programs in local Lifeline centres. Lifeline's self-help toolkit at lifeline.org.au provides resources for managing stress, anxiety, and difficult emotions. The organization runs accidental counsellor training for workplaces and community groups. Lifeline also coordinates crisis support during disasters and emergencies. Local Lifeline centres across Australia offer additional face-to-face counselling and support groups.

content.name: Línea 135 (Argentina)
content.summary: National suicide prevention service for Argentina providing 24/7 crisis support.
content.description: Línea 135 is Argentina's national suicide prevention hotline providing free, confidential crisis support 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

sections.title: About Línea 135
sections.text: Línea 135 is Argentina's national suicide prevention service operated by the Centro de Asistencia al Suicida. The service provides free, confidential crisis support to anyone in Argentina experiencing suicidal thoughts or emotional distress. Available 24/7, the hotline connects callers with trained crisis counselors who provide immediate support, crisis intervention, and connection to local mental health resources. The service has helped thousands of Argentinians through their darkest moments.

sections.title: Crisis Support
sections.text: When you call 135 in Argentina, trained crisis counselors answer and provide emotional support, crisis intervention, and help with safety planning if needed. The service is free and confidential. Counselors are trained to help with suicidal thoughts, depression, anxiety, and other emotional crises.

sections.title: Who Should Call
sections.text: Anyone in Argentina experiencing suicidal thoughts, severe depression, anxiety, or emotional crisis can call 135. Friends and family members concerned about a loved one can also call for guidance. You don't need to be in immediate danger to reach out—support is available for anyone struggling.

sections.title: How to Get Help
sections.text: Call 135 from anywhere in Argentina, available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. The service is free and confidential. For immediate medical emergencies, contact emergency services. For international crisis resources, visit Befrienders Worldwide at befrienders.org.

content.name: love is respect
content.summary: Support for young people experiencing dating abuse or unhealthy relationship patterns.

sections.title: About love is respect
sections.text: love is respect is a national resource specifically for young people ages 12-24 who are experiencing dating abuse, curious about healthy relationships, or concerned about a friend. A project of the National Domestic Violence Hotline, love is respect offers 24/7 confidential support through phone, text, and online chat. The organization provides young people with the information, tools, and support they need to recognize and navigate the complexities of dating relationships and identify early warning signs of abuse.

sections.title: How to Reach love is respect
sections.text: Call 1-866-331-9474 any time, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Text LOVEIS to 22522 for support via text message. Chat online at loveisrespect.org. TTY users can call 1-866-331-8453. Services are available in English and Spanish, with access to interpreters in over 200 languages. All contact is free and confidential. Advocates understand how to protect your safety and privacy, especially important when an abusive partner may monitor communication.

sections.title: What love is respect Offers
sections.text: When you reach out to love is respect, trained peer advocates will help you explore your relationship concerns without judgment. Advocates can help with safety planning, understanding healthy vs. unhealthy relationship dynamics, learning your options, finding local resources and support services, and building confidence in making decisions. You don't have to be in immediate danger or certain that you're experiencing abuse—love is respect is here for questions and concerns of all kinds.

sections.title: Educational Resources
sections.text: The love is respect website offers extensive resources including quizzes to help you assess your relationship (Is My Relationship Healthy?), information about different types of abuse (emotional, physical, digital, financial, sexual), guides for helping a friend in an abusive relationship, and resources for understanding consent and boundaries. Materials are specifically designed for teens and young adults and cover topics like technology safety, supporting LGBTQ+ relationships, and recognizing gaslighting and manipulation.

sections.title: Supporting a Friend
sections.text: If you're worried about a friend's relationship, love is respect provides guidance on how to have supportive conversations and what to do if someone discloses abuse to you. Advocates can help you understand what your friend might be going through and how to be supportive without making decisions for them. Remember that leaving an abusive relationship can be dangerous and complicated, and the most helpful thing you can do is listen without judgment and let your friend know you care.

content.name: National Maternal Mental Health Hotline
content.summary: 24/7 support for pregnant and postpartum individuals experiencing mental health challenges.

sections.title: About the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline
sections.text: The National Maternal Mental Health Hotline is a free, confidential, 24/7 hotline for pregnant and postpartum individuals and their families facing mental health challenges before, during, and after pregnancy. Funded by the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) and launched in 2022, the hotline provides immediate crisis support, information, referrals, and resources. Trained counselors understand the unique mental health challenges that can occur during the perinatal period.

sections.title: Who Should Call the Hotline
sections.text: Anyone experiencing emotional difficulties related to pregnancy or the postpartum period can call, including those struggling with anxiety, depression, grief after pregnancy loss, feelings of being overwhelmed, intrusive thoughts, or difficulty bonding with their baby. Partners and family members concerned about a pregnant or postpartum loved one can also call for guidance. The hotline serves people at any stage—from early pregnancy through the first year after birth—regardless of immigration status or insurance coverage.

sections.title: How to Reach the Hotline
sections.text: Call or text 1-833-9-HELP4MOMS (1-833-943-5746) any time, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Counselors are available in English and Spanish, with interpretation services available in over 60 languages. All services are free and confidential. When you call, you'll speak with a trained counselor who can provide immediate support, help you understand what you're experiencing, and connect you with appropriate resources and providers in your area.

sections.title: Services Provided
sections.text: The hotline provides crisis counseling, emotional support, information about perinatal mental health conditions, and referrals to local providers and resources. Counselors can help with safety planning if needed and provide guidance on when and how to seek additional help. The hotline can connect you with providers who specialize in perinatal mental health, support groups, and community resources. Counselors understand that perinatal mental health conditions are common, treatable, and not the parent's fault.

sections.title: Perinatal Mental Health Conditions
sections.text: The hotline provides support for all perinatal mental health conditions including prenatal depression and anxiety, postpartum depression (PPD), postpartum anxiety, postpartum OCD (intrusive thoughts about harm to baby), postpartum psychosis, birth trauma and postpartum PTSD, grief after miscarriage, stillbirth, or infant loss, and difficulties adjusting to parenthood. These conditions can affect anyone—of any background, income level, or family situation—and are among the most common complications of pregnancy.

resources.name: Mind HK

content.name: Mind HK

content.description: Mind HK provides mental health support and crisis services for Hong Kong residents through text and WhatsApp, offering accessible emotional support in English and Cantonese.

sections.title: About Mind HK
sections.text: Mind HK is a mental health charity dedicated to improving mental health awareness and support in Hong Kong. Recognizing that many people in Hong Kong face significant mental health challenges but may be reluctant to seek traditional help, Mind HK provides accessible, stigma-free support through text-based services. The organization works to promote mental health education and reduce the stigma that prevents many people from seeking help.

sections.title: Text and WhatsApp Support
sections.text: Mind HK's text support line allows anyone in Hong Kong to reach out for emotional support via SMS or WhatsApp. Text 9385 9677 to connect with trained support volunteers who can provide a listening ear and emotional support. Text-based support is ideal for those who may feel uncomfortable speaking on the phone or who need a discreet way to reach out.

sections.title: Who We Help
sections.text: Mind HK's services are available to anyone in Hong Kong experiencing emotional distress, anxiety, depression, stress, or other mental health challenges. Whether you're dealing with work pressure, relationship difficulties, family issues, or general life stress, trained volunteers are available to listen without judgment.

sections.title: How to Get Support
sections.text: To reach Mind HK's support line, text or WhatsApp 9385 9677. Trained volunteers will respond and provide emotional support in your preferred language (English or Cantonese). Visit mind.org.hk for additional mental health resources and self-help tools.

content.name: NAMI HelpLine
content.summary: Free mental health information, resources, and peer support for individuals and families.

sections.title: About the NAMI HelpLine
sections.text: The NAMI HelpLine is a free, nationwide peer-support service providing information, resource referrals, and support to people living with mental health conditions, their family members, caregivers, and the general public. NAMI (National Alliance on Mental Illness) is the nation's largest grassroots mental health organization, with over 600 local affiliates across the country dedicated to improving lives of individuals affected by mental illness through education, support, and advocacy.

sections.title: Who Should Contact the NAMI HelpLine
sections.text: The NAMI HelpLine serves anyone seeking mental health information or support. Common reasons to call include questions about mental health conditions, finding local treatment providers, navigating insurance and mental health services, connecting with support groups, learning about NAMI programs, understanding medications, coping strategies for families, and accessing crisis resources. The HelpLine is staffed by trained volunteers and staff with lived experience.

sections.title: Services Provided
sections.text: The NAMI HelpLine offers free information and referrals to local NAMI affiliates, support groups, treatment providers, and community resources. Staff can help you understand different mental health conditions, treatment options, and how to access care. They provide emotional support and can connect you with NAMI's educational programs including Family-to-Family, Peer-to-Peer, and Basics courses. The HelpLine is not a crisis line but can provide crisis resource referrals.

sections.title: How to Reach the NAMI HelpLine
sections.text: Call the NAMI HelpLine at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) Monday through Friday, 10 AM to 10 PM Eastern Time. You can also text NAMI to 741741 for 24/7 crisis support through Crisis Text Line. Email inquiries can be sent to info@nami.org. Visit nami.org to find your local NAMI affiliate, access educational resources, join support groups, and learn about advocacy opportunities.

sections.title: NAMI Educational Programs
sections.text: NAMI offers free evidence-based educational programs including Family-to-Family (an 8-session course for families and caregivers), Peer-to-Peer (for adults living with mental health conditions), NAMI Basics (for parents and caregivers of children), and Homefront (for military families). These programs are taught by trained peers who have personal experience with mental illness. NAMI also runs thousands of support groups nationwide where people can share experiences in a safe environment.

sections.title: NAMI Advocacy
sections.text: NAMI advocates for better policies, services, and funding for mental health at local, state, and federal levels. The organization works to improve access to mental health care, fight discrimination against people with mental illness, and ensure that mental health is treated equally with physical health. NAMI mobilizes its network of advocates to contact legislators, participate in awareness campaigns, and share personal stories to change hearts and minds about mental illness. Members can join advocacy efforts through NAMI's grassroots network.

sections.title: Find Your Local NAMI
sections.text: NAMI has over 600 local affiliates across the United States, each providing programs and services tailored to their community. Local affiliates offer in-person support groups, educational classes, community outreach, and connections to local mental health resources. To find your local NAMI affiliate, visit nami.org and enter your zip code. Local affiliates are often staffed by volunteers with personal experience with mental illness who can provide peer support and guidance on navigating the mental health system in your area.

content.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline
content.summary: 24/7 confidential support for survivors of domestic and intimate partner violence and their loved ones.

sections.title: About The National Domestic Violence Hotline
sections.text: The National Domestic Violence Hotline (also known as The Hotline) is a nonprofit organization that provides crisis intervention, safety planning, information, and referrals to victims and survivors of domestic violence, their friends, and families. Operating 24/7 since 1996, The Hotline has answered millions of calls and helped countless people take their first steps toward safety and healing.

sections.title: Who Should Reach Out
sections.text: The Hotline serves anyone experiencing domestic violence, dating abuse, or stalking, as well as friends, family members, and co-workers who want to help a loved one. You can reach out whether you're in immediate danger, planning to leave an abusive relationship, already left but need support, or just need someone to talk to about your situation. There is no wrong reason to call.

sections.title: How to Contact The Hotline
sections.text: Call 1-800-799-SAFE (7233) available 24/7, 365 days a year. Text START to 88788. Chat online at thehotline.org. TTY users can call 1-800-787-3224. Services are available in English and Spanish, with access to interpreters in over 200 languages. All contact is confidential, and advocates understand how to protect your safety and privacy.

sections.title: What to Expect When You Contact The Hotline
sections.text: When you reach out, a trained advocate will listen without judgment and help you explore your options. Advocates can help with safety planning, understanding the dynamics of abuse, exploring your options, finding local resources such as shelters and legal services, and emotional support. You don't have to make any decisions during the call—advocates are there to support you wherever you are in your journey.

sections.title: Safety Planning Resources
sections.text: The Hotline website offers safety planning resources including tips for staying safe while in a relationship, how to safely leave, digital safety and privacy protection, and information about protective orders. Advocates can help create a personalized safety plan that addresses your specific situation. If you're using a shared device, learn how to clear your browsing history to protect your privacy.

content.name: Postpartum Support International (PSI)
content.summary: Support and resources for perinatal mood and anxiety disorders including postpartum depression.

sections.title: About Postpartum Support International
sections.text: Postpartum Support International (PSI) is a nonprofit organization dedicated to helping families suffering from perinatal mood and anxiety disorders, including postpartum depression. Founded in 1987, PSI provides direct peer support, educates healthcare professionals, and advocates for improved awareness and treatment. PSI's mission is to ensure that no family suffering from a perinatal mental health condition feels alone. The organization operates in all 50 states and over 40 countries.

sections.title: PSI Helpline
sections.text: PSI operates a confidential helpline at 1-800-944-4773 (English and Spanish) where you can leave a message and receive a return call within 24-48 hours from a trained volunteer who has personal experience with perinatal mental health conditions. For immediate crisis support, text HOME to 741741 to reach the Crisis Text Line. The PSI helpline is not a crisis line but provides warm, peer-based support and connections to local resources and providers who specialize in perinatal mental health.

sections.title: Perinatal Mental Health Conditions
sections.text: PSI provides resources for a range of perinatal mood and anxiety disorders including postpartum depression (PPD), postpartum anxiety, postpartum OCD, postpartum psychosis, postpartum PTSD, and pregnancy/prenatal depression and anxiety. These conditions can affect anyone during pregnancy or up to a year after birth—including fathers, partners, and adoptive parents. PSI emphasizes that perinatal mood disorders are common, temporary with proper treatment, and not the parent's fault.

sections.title: Support Groups and Coordinators
sections.text: PSI maintains a network of volunteer coordinators in every state and many countries who can connect you with local support groups, providers, and resources. Online support groups meet weekly via video conference, allowing parents to connect with others going through similar experiences regardless of location. Support groups are peer-led and provide a confidential space to share struggles, celebrate progress, and learn coping strategies. Groups are available in English and Spanish, with some groups specifically for fathers and partners.

sections.title: Finding Treatment Providers
sections.text: PSI's provider directory helps families find therapists, psychiatrists, and other mental health professionals who specialize in perinatal mental health. The organization also offers professional training certification for clinicians who want to specialize in treating perinatal mood disorders. PSI's website includes educational materials for healthcare providers on screening, diagnosis, and treatment of perinatal mental health conditions, helping ensure families receive appropriate evidence-based care.

content.name: RAINN National Sexual Assault Hotline
content.summary: 24/7 confidential support for survivors of sexual assault and their loved ones.

sections.title: About RAINN and the National Sexual Assault Hotline
sections.text: RAINN (Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network) is the nation's largest anti-sexual violence organization. RAINN operates the National Sexual Assault Hotline, the Department of Defense Safe Helpline, and public education programs. Since its founding in 1994, RAINN has helped more than 3 million survivors of sexual violence and their loved ones. The organization also works to improve policies and practices around sexual violence prevention and response.

sections.title: Who Should Reach Out
sections.text: The RAINN hotline serves survivors of sexual assault, abuse, and incest, as well as their friends, family members, and loved ones. You can reach out whether the assault happened recently or years ago. Common reasons to contact RAINN include processing a recent assault, seeking support for past trauma, finding local resources and counseling, understanding your options for reporting, getting help for a loved one, and learning about the healing process.

sections.title: How to Contact RAINN
sections.text: Call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) available 24/7. Chat online at rainn.org/get-help for confidential support. The hotline automatically connects you to a local sexual assault service provider based on your area code. Staff members are trained support specialists who provide crisis support, information about medical care, and referrals to local resources. Services are available in English and Spanish.

sections.title: What to Expect When You Call
sections.text: When you contact RAINN, a trained staff member will listen without judgment and help you understand your options. They can provide emotional support, information about the effects of sexual violence, guidance on reporting options, referrals to local hospitals and counseling services, and information about the legal process. You control the conversation and are not required to share any information you're not comfortable sharing.

sections.title: Additional RAINN Resources
sections.text: Beyond crisis support, RAINN offers educational resources about consent, healthy relationships, and preventing sexual violence. The RAINN website includes information about the effects of sexual violence, self-care strategies for survivors, guidance for supporting loved ones, and state-by-state information about statutes of limitations and victims' rights. RAINN also operates the DoD Safe Helpline for military members affected by sexual assault.

resources.title: Samaritans Singapore

content.name: Samaritans Singapore
content.summary: 24/7 emotional support line for anyone in Singapore.
content.description: Samaritans of Singapore (SOS) provides 24-hour crisis support and suicide prevention services through their hotline, reaching anyone in Singapore who needs emotional support.

sections.title: About Samaritans of Singapore
sections.text: Samaritans of Singapore (SOS) is a non-religious, non-profit organization providing 24-hour confidential emotional support for anyone in crisis or experiencing suicidal thoughts. Established in 1969, SOS is Singapore's only 24-hour emotional support line. The organization is dedicated to providing a listening ear to anyone who needs it. SOS has trained thousands of volunteers over the decades and has supported countless Singaporeans through their most difficult moments.

sections.title: Crisis Support Services
sections.text: SOS operates a 24-hour hotline at 1-767 (1-SOS), staffed by trained volunteers who provide non-judgmental listening support. Callers can discuss any issue causing emotional distress, from suicidal thoughts to relationship problems, work stress, or general life difficulties. The service is completely confidential.

sections.title: Who Can Call
sections.text: Anyone in Singapore can call SOS. You don't need to be suicidal to reach out—SOS supports anyone experiencing emotional distress. Common reasons people call include depression, anxiety, loneliness, relationship issues, work or school stress, family problems, and grief.

sections.title: How to Get Help
sections.text: Call 1-767 anytime, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. SOS also provides email support at pat@sos.org.sg for those who prefer written communication. Visit sos.org.sg for additional resources and information about suicide prevention. Remember, seeking help is a sign of strength.

content.name: Samaritans (UK & Ireland)
content.summary: 24/7 emotional support line for anyone in distress or experiencing suicidal thoughts.

sections.title: About Samaritans
sections.text: Samaritans is a registered charity aimed at providing emotional support to anyone in emotional distress, struggling to cope, or at risk of suicide throughout the United Kingdom and Republic of Ireland. Founded in 1953 by Reverend Chad Varah in London, Samaritans pioneered the concept of crisis helplines. The organization operates with a simple vision: fewer people die by suicide. Samaritans believes that having someone to talk to, without judgment, can be life-changing and potentially life-saving.

sections.title: Who Should Contact Samaritans
sections.text: You can contact Samaritans about anything that's troubling you, no matter how large or small the issue feels. You don't have to be suicidal to reach out—Samaritans is there for anyone struggling to cope, feeling overwhelmed, worried about someone else, or just needing someone to talk to. Common reasons people contact Samaritans include relationship problems, loss and bereavement, financial worries, mental health concerns, loneliness, and thoughts of suicide. Whatever you're going through, Samaritans volunteers will listen without judgment.

sections.title: How to Contact Samaritans
sections.text: Call 116 123 free from any phone, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. This number is free to call from landlines and mobiles in the UK and Ireland. You can also email jo@samaritans.org and receive a response within 24 hours. In-person visits are available at local Samaritans branches—visit samaritans.org to find your nearest branch and opening hours. Welsh speakers can call the Welsh Language Line on 0808 164 0123 (7pm-11pm daily). Samaritans also offers a self-help app with guided exercises for emotional support.

sections.title: What Happens When You Contact Samaritans
sections.text: When you contact Samaritans, you'll speak with a trained volunteer who will give you the time and space to talk about what's on your mind. Volunteers practice active listening—they won't judge you, give advice, or tell you what to do. Instead, they help you explore your feelings and thoughts at your own pace. Calls are confidential and won't appear on your phone bill in a way that identifies Samaritans. You can remain anonymous if you wish. There's no time limit on calls, and you can contact Samaritans as often as you need.

sections.title: Additional Samaritans Services
sections.text: Beyond the helpline, Samaritans runs programs to support mental health across communities. The Listener Training helps volunteers develop skills for providing emotional support. Samaritans partners with Network Rail, schools, prisons, and workplaces to train staff in suicide prevention. The Step by Step service supports schools after a suspected suicide. Samaritans also works to reduce harmful media portrayal of suicide and advocated for the Suicide Prevention Act. The organization trains thousands of new volunteers each year to ensure support is always available.

content.name: SAMHSA National Helpline
content.summary: 24/7 free treatment referral and information for mental health and substance use disorders.

sections.title: About the SAMHSA National Helpline
sections.text: The SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-HELP) is a free, confidential, 24/7, 365-day-a-year treatment referral and information service provided by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. The helpline provides referrals to local treatment facilities, support groups, and community-based organizations, as well as information about mental health and substance use disorders, prevention, and recovery.

sections.title: Who Should Call
sections.text: The SAMHSA Helpline serves individuals and family members facing mental health or substance use disorders. Common reasons to call include finding treatment for addiction or mental health issues, learning about treatment options and what to expect, getting help for a family member, finding support groups in your area, understanding insurance coverage for treatment, and getting information about recovery resources.

sections.title: Services Provided
sections.text: Information specialists answer calls 24/7 and can provide referrals to treatment facilities, information about treatment and recovery, and support group locations. The helpline can assist with finding treatment that fits your needs, including options for people without insurance or with limited coverage. Information specialists can also provide information about the types of treatment available, what to expect in treatment, and how to support someone in recovery.

sections.title: Treatment Locator
sections.text: SAMHSA's online treatment locator at findtreatment.gov allows you to search for treatment facilities by location, type of treatment, and services offered. You can filter by substance use treatment, mental health services, crisis services, and other criteria. The database includes thousands of treatment programs across the United States. The helpline staff can also help you use this resource.

sections.title: Privacy and Confidentiality
sections.text: Calls to the SAMHSA Helpline are free and confidential. The helpline is available in English and Spanish. TTY service is available at 1-800-487-4889. You do not need to provide your name or any personal information to receive help. The service is anonymous, and caller information is not reported to law enforcement or other agencies.
