resources.description: SOS Voz Amiga provides free, confidential emotional support by phone for anyone in Portugal experiencing emotional distress, loneliness, or crisis.

content.name: SOS Voz Amiga (Portugal)
content.summary: Emotional support helpline for anyone in Portugal experiencing distress.
content.description: SOS Voz Amiga provides free, confidential emotional support by phone for anyone in Portugal experiencing emotional distress, loneliness, or crisis.

sections.title: About SOS Voz Amiga
sections.text: SOS Voz Amiga is a Portuguese nonprofit organization that provides free, confidential emotional support to anyone experiencing distress. Operating since 1978, the organization is staffed by trained volunteers who offer a compassionate listening ear to people dealing with loneliness, depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and other emotional challenges. The organization is part of the international Befrienders network and has helped thousands of Portuguese residents find hope and support.

sections.title: Phone Support
sections.text: SOS Voz Amiga's helpline at 213 544 545 connects callers with trained volunteers who provide non-judgmental emotional support. The service is available during scheduled hours—check the website for current availability. Calls are confidential, and callers can remain anonymous.

sections.title: Who Can Use the Service
sections.text: Anyone in Portugal can call SOS Voz Amiga. The service welcomes calls from people experiencing any form of emotional distress, including depression, anxiety, loneliness, relationship problems, grief, work stress, or thoughts of suicide.

sections.title: How to Get Support
sections.text: Call 213 544 545 during operating hours to speak with a trained volunteer. The service is free and confidential. Visit sosvozamiga.org for additional resources and information about getting help. For immediate life-threatening emergencies, contact Portuguese emergency services at 112.

content.name: StrongHearts Native Helpline
content.summary: Culturally-appropriate domestic and dating violence support for Native Americans and Alaska Natives.

sections.title: About the StrongHearts Native Helpline
sections.text: The StrongHearts Native Helpline is a culturally-appropriate and confidential domestic, dating, and sexual violence helpline for Native Americans and Alaska Natives. Launched in 2017 as a partnership between the National Indigenous Women's Resource Center and the National Domestic Violence Hotline, StrongHearts is staffed by advocates who understand tribal cultures and the unique barriers and challenges facing Native communities. The helpline honors Indigenous values while providing compassionate support and connections to Native-centered resources.

sections.title: Who the Helpline Serves
sections.text: StrongHearts serves Native Americans, Alaska Natives, and anyone in a relationship with a Native person who is experiencing domestic violence, dating violence, or sexual violence. You can call if you're in a crisis situation, planning to leave an abusive relationship, already left but need support, or are concerned about a family member or friend. The helpline also serves those who have experienced historical trauma, family violence, or community violence. Anyone can call regardless of their enrollment status or tribal affiliation.

sections.title: How to Reach the Helpline
sections.text: Call 1-844-7NATIVE (1-844-762-8483) to speak with a trained advocate. The helpline operates 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Chat support is available through the StrongHearts website at strongheartshelpline.org. Services are provided in English, with interpretation available for other languages including many Native languages. All services are free and confidential. Advocates are trained in Native-centered advocacy and understand the complexities of tribal jurisdiction and resources.

sections.title: Services Provided
sections.text: StrongHearts advocates provide crisis intervention, safety planning, information about domestic violence, and referrals to Native-centered resources including tribal programs, tribal courts, and culturally-specific services. Advocates can help navigate the unique jurisdictional complexities that Native survivors face, including matters involving tribal, state, and federal law. The helpline provides peer support and guidance while respecting the importance of extended family and community in Native cultures.

sections.title: Resources for Native Communities
sections.text: StrongHearts works closely with the National Indigenous Women's Resource Center (NIWRC), which provides additional resources specifically for Native communities. These include information about tribal domestic violence programs, sexual assault service providers, and culturally-specific healing resources. Educational materials address the intersection of domestic violence with historical trauma, Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women (MMIW), and other issues affecting Native communities. Resources are designed to support both survivors and advocates working in tribal communities.

content.name: Talk Suicide Canada
content.summary: National 988 crisis service for Canada providing suicide prevention and crisis support.

sections.title: About Talk Suicide Canada
sections.text: Talk Suicide Canada is the national crisis service providing 24/7 support for anyone who is having thoughts of suicide or is worried about someone who may be. Launched with the three-digit 988 number in 2023, Talk Suicide Canada connects people across the country with trained responders who can provide immediate support, crisis intervention, and connections to local resources. The service is operated by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) in partnership with crisis centres across Canada.

sections.title: Who Should Contact 988
sections.text: Call or text 988 if you are having thoughts of suicide, are worried about someone who may be considering suicide, are experiencing a mental health crisis, or need emotional support. You don't have to be in immediate danger to reach out—988 is there for anyone who needs someone to talk to about their mental health. Friends and family members concerned about a loved one can also call for guidance on how to help.

sections.title: How to Reach Talk Suicide Canada
sections.text: Call or text 988 from anywhere in Canada, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Service is available in English and French. When you call, you'll be connected with a trained responder who will listen, provide support, and help you through the crisis. For those who prefer text-based communication, texting 988 connects you with the same crisis support. The service is free and confidential.

sections.title: What Happens When You Contact 988
sections.text: When you call or text 988, a trained crisis responder will answer and listen without judgment. They will work with you to understand your situation, provide emotional support, help with safety planning if needed, and connect you with local resources and services. Calls are confidential, and responders will only involve emergency services if there is an immediate threat to your safety. You can remain anonymous if you choose.

sections.title: Additional Resources
sections.text: Beyond 988, the Talk Suicide Canada website (talksuicide.ca) provides resources including information about suicide prevention, how to support someone in crisis, and links to provincial and territorial crisis services. Resources are available for specific populations including Indigenous peoples, youth, and 2SLGBTQ+ communities. The website also provides guidance for those who have lost someone to suicide and resources for communities affected by suicide.

content.name: The Trevor Project
content.summary: 24/7 crisis support for LGBTQ+ young people experiencing mental health crisis or suicidal thoughts.

sections.title: About The Trevor Project
sections.text: The Trevor Project is the world's largest suicide prevention and mental health organization for LGBTQ+ young people. Founded in 1998 after the Academy Award-winning short film 'Trevor,' the organization provides 24/7 crisis intervention and suicide prevention services to LGBTQ+ young people under 25 through phone, text, and chat. The Trevor Project has answered millions of contacts and trains thousands of counselors each year.

sections.title: Who Should Reach Out
sections.text: The Trevor Project serves LGBTQ+ young people under 25 who are experiencing crisis, thinking about suicide, or simply need someone to talk to. Common reasons to reach out include feeling isolated, experiencing rejection from family or friends, dealing with bullying, questioning gender identity or sexual orientation, struggling with anxiety or depression, or needing support during difficult times. You don't have to identify any specific way to reach out.

sections.title: How to Contact The Trevor Project
sections.text: Call the TrevorLifeline at 1-866-488-7386 available 24/7. Text START to 678-678 for TrevorText. Chat online at TheTrevorProject.org/get-help. All services are free, confidential, and staffed by trained LGBTQ+ counselors who understand your experiences. Average wait times are typically under 5 minutes. Spanish-speaking support is available.

sections.title: TrevorSpace Online Community
sections.text: Beyond crisis services, The Trevor Project offers TrevorSpace, an affirming international online community for LGBTQ+ young people ages 13-24. TrevorSpace is a monitored social networking site where young people can connect with peers, share their stories, find support, and access resources in a safe environment. The community has helped thousands of LGBTQ+ youth feel less alone.

sections.title: Education and Training
sections.text: The Trevor Project provides free educational resources including guides for parents of LGBTQ+ youth, resources for educators and schools, workplace training programs, and research on LGBTQ+ youth mental health. Their annual National Survey on LGBTQ+ Youth Mental Health provides vital data that informs policy and programs. The organization also advocates for LGBTQ+ youth at local, state, and federal levels.

content.name: Trans Lifeline
content.summary: Peer support hotline run by and for trans people experiencing crisis or needing emotional support.

sections.title: About Trans Lifeline
sections.text: Trans Lifeline is a grassroots peer support hotline run by and for transgender people. Founded in 2014, it is the only trans-led crisis hotline in the United States and Canada. All operators are transgender and understand the unique challenges facing the trans community. Trans Lifeline operates on a consent-based model that prioritizes caller autonomy and does not engage in non-consensual active rescue practices.

sections.title: Who Should Call
sections.text: Trans Lifeline serves transgender and questioning individuals of any age experiencing emotional crisis, suicidal thoughts, or simply needing support from someone who understands. Common reasons to call include navigating transition, dealing with family rejection, experiencing discrimination or harassment, feeling isolated, processing complex emotions about gender identity, or needing help accessing trans-specific resources.

sections.title: How to Contact Trans Lifeline
sections.text: Call 1-877-565-8860 (US) or 1-877-330-6366 (Canada). The hotline is available 24/7, though staffing levels vary. Wait times may be longer during overnight hours. All calls are answered by transgender peer support operators. The service is free and confidential. Trans Lifeline does not trace calls or contact emergency services without explicit consent.

sections.title: Trans Lifeline Microgrants
sections.text: Trans Lifeline offers microgrants to help trans people access name changes, updated identity documents, and other transition-related needs. The organization has distributed thousands of grants to help trans people obtain legal documents that match their gender identity. These grants help reduce barriers to accessing affirming documents, employment, and housing.

sections.title: Support for Family and Friends
sections.text: Trans Lifeline also provides support for family members, friends, and allies of transgender people who want to better understand and support their loved ones. Operators can provide resources, answer questions, and offer guidance on how to be supportive. The organization's website includes educational materials about transgender experiences and how to be an ally.

content.name: Veterans Crisis Line
content.summary: 24/7 confidential crisis support for Veterans, service members, National Guard, Reserve, and their families.

sections.title: About the Veterans Crisis Line
sections.text: The Veterans Crisis Line is a free, confidential resource available to anyone, including Veterans, service members, National Guard and Reserve members, and those who support them. Operated by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, the Veterans Crisis Line connects callers with specially trained responders who understand the unique experiences and challenges faced by those who have served. Since its launch in 2007, the Veterans Crisis Line has answered millions of calls and dispatched emergency services to Veterans in imminent crisis.

sections.title: Who Should Contact the Veterans Crisis Line
sections.text: The Veterans Crisis Line serves all Veterans, including those who served in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Marines, Coast Guard, Space Force, and National Guard or Reserve. You do not need to be enrolled in VA benefits or health care to use this service. Family members and friends concerned about a Veteran can also call for guidance on how to help. You should reach out if you're having thoughts of suicide, experiencing emotional distress, struggling with PTSD symptoms, facing a personal crisis, or simply need someone to talk to who understands military service.

sections.title: How to Reach the Veterans Crisis Line
sections.text: Call 988 and Press 1 to connect with a trained VA responder. You can also text 838255 to reach a crisis counselor via text message. For online chat support, visit veteranscrisisline.net and click the chat button. TTY users can call 1-800-799-4889. Support is available in English and Spanish, with language interpretation services available for other languages. All contact methods are available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year.

sections.title: What Happens When You Reach Out
sections.text: When you contact the Veterans Crisis Line, you will be connected with a trained responder, many of whom are Veterans themselves. They will listen without judgment and work with you to understand your situation. Responders can provide immediate crisis intervention, safety planning, and connections to local resources. If you're in immediate danger, they can coordinate with local emergency services. All conversations are confidential, and you can remain anonymous if you choose. The goal is to help you through the crisis and connect you with ongoing support.

sections.title: Additional VA Mental Health Resources
sections.text: Beyond the Crisis Line, the VA offers extensive mental health services including PTSD treatment programs, counseling at Vet Centers (community-based centers staffed by combat Veterans), the Veteran Readjustment Counseling program, and various evidence-based treatments for depression, anxiety, and trauma. The VA's Make the Connection website (maketheconnection.net) features stories from Veterans who have faced mental health challenges and found support. Many Veterans find that connecting with others who share similar experiences is an important part of their recovery journey.

content.name: YouthLine
content.summary: Teen-to-teen crisis support line where young people help other young people.

sections.title: About YouthLine
sections.text: YouthLine is a teen-to-teen crisis support service where young people help other young people navigate difficult times. Operated by Lines for Life, YouthLine is staffed by trained teen volunteers who provide peer support, crisis intervention, and referrals to youth ages 11-21. The unique peer-to-peer model recognizes that young people often prefer talking to someone their own age who understands their experiences, making YouthLine an accessible entry point for youth seeking help.

sections.title: Who Can Contact YouthLine
sections.text: YouthLine serves young people ages 11-21 who are struggling with any issue—you don't have to be in crisis to reach out. Common reasons youth contact YouthLine include stress, anxiety, depression, relationship problems, family conflict, bullying, identity questions, grief, suicidal thoughts, and simply needing someone to talk to. If you're a young person who needs support but isn't sure where to turn, YouthLine's peer counselors are here to listen without judgment.

sections.title: How to Reach YouthLine
sections.text: Call 1-877-968-8491 to talk with a teen peer counselor. Teen volunteers answer calls from 4 PM to 10 PM Pacific Time, Monday through Friday, and 6 PM to 10 PM Pacific Time on weekends. Outside these hours, trained adult volunteers provide support. You can also text teen2teen to 839863, chat online at oregonyouthline.org, or email help@oregonyouthline.org. All services are free and confidential.

sections.title: Teen Volunteer Counselors
sections.text: YouthLine's teen helpers are high school students who complete an extensive training program covering crisis intervention, active listening, mental health awareness, and suicide prevention. Teen volunteers bring lived experience of adolescent challenges while receiving professional supervision and support. The peer model reduces barriers to seeking help—many young people find it easier to open up to someone their own age who can genuinely relate to their experiences with school, relationships, and growing up.

sections.title: Beyond the Line
sections.text: YouthLine offers more than crisis support. The website provides self-help resources, information about mental health, and tips for supporting friends in crisis. YouthLine also runs school-based programs that train students in peer support and suicide prevention. If you're a young person interested in helping others, YouthLine offers volunteer opportunities for teens who want to make a difference in their community by supporting their peers.

content.name: Alcoholics Anonymous (AA)
content.description: Free 12-step fellowship for alcohol recovery. Find meetings worldwide, both in-person and online.

sections.title: About Alcoholics Anonymous
sections.text: Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) is an international fellowship of people who have had a drinking problem. Founded in 1935, AA is a nonprofessional, self-supporting, multiracial, apolitical organization open to anyone who wants to stop drinking. The only requirement for membership is a desire to stop drinking. AA has helped millions of people achieve and maintain sobriety through its 12-step program and peer support meetings.

sections.title: How AA Works
sections.text: AA's program of recovery is based on 12 Steps and 12 Traditions. Members work through these steps with the support of a sponsor (a more experienced member) and the fellowship of other recovering alcoholics. The program emphasizes honesty, acceptance, and spiritual growth. While AA has spiritual elements, it is not affiliated with any religion, and members define their own concept of a higher power.

sections.title: Finding Meetings
sections.text: AA meetings are held throughout the world, with hundreds of thousands of groups meeting in-person and online. Visit aa.org/find-aa to search for meetings by location. Meeting types include open meetings (anyone can attend) and closed meetings (for alcoholics only), speaker meetings, discussion meetings, and Big Book study groups. Online meetings are available 24/7 for those who cannot attend in person.

sections.title: What to Expect at Your First Meeting
sections.text: At an AA meeting, you'll find a group of people who understand what you're going through. Meetings typically last an hour and may include readings, personal sharing, and discussion. You're never required to speak if you're not comfortable. Many newcomers feel nervous at first, but most report feeling welcomed and supported. Some people attend many meetings before deciding if AA is right for them.

sections.title: Getting Started
sections.text: If you're wondering whether you have a drinking problem, AA suggests taking a self-assessment questionnaire available on their website. You can attend meetings as a visitor before deciding to join. There are no dues or fees for AA membership. The organization is entirely self-supporting through voluntary member contributions. Many areas have local AA hotlines where you can speak with a recovering alcoholic.

content.name: Active Minds
content.description: Student-led mental health awareness and advocacy organization. Chapters on college campuses nationwide.

sections.title: About Active Minds
sections.text: Active Minds is the nation's premier nonprofit organization supporting mental health awareness and education for young adults. Founded in 2003, Active Minds empowers students to speak openly about mental health to reduce stigma and create lasting change on college campuses. The organization has chapters at over 1,000 high schools, colleges, and universities across the United States and internationally.

sections.title: Campus Chapters
sections.text: Active Minds chapters are student-led groups that promote mental health awareness through campus events, peer education, and advocacy initiatives. Chapters host events like Send Silence Packing (a traveling exhibit on suicide awareness), stress relief activities during finals, and discussions about mental health. Students can start a new chapter at their school or join an existing one.

sections.title: Programs and Initiatives
sections.text: Active Minds offers training programs including Mental Health First Aid, gatekeeper training for identifying students in distress, and leadership development for chapter officers. The organization runs awareness campaigns like Active Minds Week, provides curriculum for mental health education, and advocates for policies that support student mental health on campus and nationally.

sections.title: Resources for Students
sections.text: Active Minds provides free resources for students including guides on finding campus mental health services, information about common mental health challenges in college, tips for supporting friends in distress, and self-care strategies. The website includes personal stories from students who have faced mental health challenges and found support through Active Minds.

sections.title: How to Get Involved
sections.text: Students can get involved with Active Minds by joining a local chapter, starting a new chapter at their school, participating in campus events, or becoming a Send Silence Packing volunteer. The organization also offers internships, leadership programs, and opportunities to share your story to help reduce mental health stigma among young people.

sections.title: About ADAA
sections.text: The Anxiety and Depression Association of America (ADAA) is an international nonprofit organization dedicated to the prevention, treatment, and cure of anxiety, depression, OCD, PTSD, and related disorders. Founded in 1979, ADAA works to improve the lives of millions of people affected by these conditions through education, research funding, and support for mental health professionals and the public.

sections.title: Educational Resources
sections.text: ADAA provides extensive free educational resources including articles, webinars, podcasts, and videos about anxiety disorders, depression, and related conditions. Topics cover symptoms, treatment options, self-help strategies, and the latest research findings. Resources are written and reviewed by mental health professionals and help people understand their conditions and make informed treatment decisions.

sections.title: Find a Therapist Directory
sections.text: ADAA maintains a searchable directory of licensed mental health professionals who specialize in treating anxiety disorders and depression. You can search by location, specialty, and treatment approach including cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), exposure therapy, and medication management. All listed providers have expertise in evidence-based treatments for anxiety and mood disorders.

sections.title: Online Peer Support Community
sections.text: ADAA offers a moderated online peer support community where people with anxiety and depression can connect, share experiences, and support each other. The community provides a safe space to discuss challenges, celebrate progress, and feel less alone. Members can participate in discussion forums, read personal stories, and access peer-driven resources.

sections.title: For Mental Health Professionals
sections.text: ADAA supports mental health professionals through continuing education opportunities, research grants, and an annual conference that brings together leading researchers and clinicians. The organization publishes the peer-reviewed journal Depression and Anxiety and provides resources to help clinicians deliver evidence-based treatment for anxiety and mood disorders.

sections.title: About Al-Anon Family Groups
sections.text: Al-Anon Family Groups is a worldwide fellowship of people who have been affected by someone else's drinking. Founded in 1951 by Lois Wilson and Anne B., wives of early Alcoholics Anonymous members, Al-Anon offers a program of recovery based on the Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions. The organization helps families and friends of alcoholics find understanding, strength, and hope through shared experiences. Al-Anon is not affiliated with any religious organization, political group, or institution.

sections.title: Who Al-Anon Is For
sections.text: Al-Anon welcomes anyone whose life has been affected by someone else's drinking, whether that person is still drinking, has stopped, has passed away, or is no longer in their life. This includes spouses, partners, parents, children, siblings, friends, and coworkers. Alateen, a part of Al-Anon, is specifically for teenagers affected by a family member's drinking. You don't need to wait for someone to hit rock bottom or seek treatment—Al-Anon focuses on your own well-being regardless of what the drinker chooses to do.

sections.title: How Al-Anon Works
sections.text: Al-Anon meetings provide a safe, confidential environment where members share their experiences and learn from each other. The program centers on the Three Cs: You didn't Cause the alcoholism, you can't Cure it, and you can't Control it. Members learn to detach with love, set healthy boundaries, and focus on their own recovery. The Twelve Steps guide personal growth, while sponsors (experienced members) offer one-on-one support. Members discover they are not alone and that recovery is possible for them regardless of whether the alcoholic chooses to get help.

sections.title: Finding Al-Anon Meetings
sections.text: Al-Anon has over 24,000 groups meeting in 133 countries worldwide. Meetings are held in-person at community centers, churches, hospitals, and other locations, as well as online through Al-Anon's Electronic Meeting platform. To find meetings near you, visit al-anon.org and use the meeting finder tool. Meeting types include speaker meetings, discussion meetings, and step study groups. First-time visitors are always welcome—there's no registration or commitment required. Many groups welcome newcomers with special beginner meetings or literature.

sections.title: Getting Started with Al-Anon
sections.text: If you're new to Al-Anon, consider attending at least six different meetings before deciding if the program is right for you—each meeting has its own personality. Al-Anon has no dues or fees; groups are self-supporting through voluntary contributions. Free literature including pamphlets, books, and daily readers are available at meetings and through the Al-Anon website. The Al-Anon app provides meeting information, daily readings, and connection to the worldwide fellowship. Remember that everything shared at meetings is confidential.

sections.title: About ASAN
sections.text: The Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN) is a nonprofit organization run by and for autistic people. Founded in 2006, ASAN seeks to advance the principles of the disability rights movement in the world of autism. The organization's motto—'Nothing About Us Without Us'—reflects its commitment to ensuring autistic people have a meaningful voice in all discussions and decisions that affect their lives. ASAN advocates for systemic change rather than individual cure, promoting acceptance and inclusion of neurodivergent individuals.

sections.title: Policy and Advocacy Work
sections.text: ASAN engages in advocacy at local, state, and federal levels on issues affecting autistic people. Key priorities include opposing the institutionalization of disabled people, promoting community-based services and supports, ensuring educational inclusion, protecting voting rights, advocating for accessible healthcare, and opposing practices like seclusion, restraint, and aversive interventions. ASAN played a key role in passing the ABLE Act and opposes organizations that promote autism 'cures' or frame autism as a tragedy.

sections.title: Educational Resources
sections.text: ASAN produces educational resources written by autistic people for autistic people and their allies. Publications include plain language guides about healthcare, voting, self-advocacy, and navigating systems. The organization provides toolkits on topics like employment, education rights, and healthcare access. Resources emphasize the value of autistic perspectives and the neurodiversity paradigm—the understanding that neurological differences like autism are natural variations rather than defects to be cured.

sections.title: Autistic Community
sections.text: ASAN connects autistic people with a broader community of self-advocates. The organization hosts online forums and community spaces, supports local self-advocacy groups, and provides training for autistic leaders. ASAN's annual Disability Day of Mourning events commemorate disabled people killed by their caregivers and highlight the need for systemic change. The organization emphasizes that autistic people are the experts on their own experiences and should lead conversations about autism.

sections.title: Getting Involved
sections.text: Autistic individuals and allies can get involved with ASAN in various ways. You can sign up for action alerts to participate in advocacy campaigns, share your story to help inform policy work, access free resources for self-advocacy, and follow ASAN's work on issues affecting the autistic community. ASAN also welcomes volunteers and provides internship opportunities. Whether you're newly diagnosed, a longtime self-advocate, or a non-autistic ally, ASAN offers ways to connect and contribute.

sections.title: About Asian Mental Health Collective
sections.text: The Asian Mental Health Collective (AMHC) is a nonprofit organization dedicated to normalizing and de-stigmatizing mental health within the Asian community. Founded to address the significant barriers Asian and Asian American individuals face in accessing culturally competent mental health care, AMHC provides resources, education, and a therapist directory to help community members find support that understands their cultural background. The organization serves the diverse Asian diaspora including East Asian, Southeast Asian, South Asian, and Pacific Islander communities.

sections.title: Finding an Asian Therapist
sections.text: AMHC maintains a comprehensive directory of mental health professionals who identify as Asian or specialize in serving Asian communities. The directory allows you to search by location, specialty, language, and Asian identity to find a therapist who understands your cultural context. Providers in the directory are trained mental health professionals who recognize the unique cultural factors—including family dynamics, model minority myth pressures, immigration experiences, and intergenerational trauma—that may impact Asian clients' mental health.

sections.title: Culturally Relevant Resources
sections.text: AMHC provides educational resources that address mental health through an Asian cultural lens. Articles and guides cover topics like navigating family expectations, addressing stigma about therapy within Asian families, understanding how cultural values affect mental health, managing acculturation stress, and communicating about mental health with parents who may have different beliefs. Resources acknowledge that many Asian cultures have historically stigmatized mental health issues, and offer strategies for breaking down these barriers.

sections.title: Community and Storytelling
sections.text: AMHC creates space for Asian individuals to share their mental health stories and connect with a community that understands their experiences. The organization features personal narratives from Asian Americans about their mental health journeys, helping normalize seeking help within communities where mental health discussions have been taboo. By amplifying these voices, AMHC helps reduce shame and isolation while showing that recovery and healing are possible.

sections.title: Advocacy and Awareness
sections.text: AMHC works to improve mental health awareness and access within Asian communities through education, partnerships, and advocacy. The organization collaborates with schools, universities, and community organizations to provide culturally responsive mental health education. AMHC participates in Asian American mental health awareness initiatives and advocates for increased representation of Asian providers and culturally competent care options. The goal is a future where all Asian individuals can access mental health support without stigma.

sections.title: About the Autism Society
sections.text: The Autism Society is the nation's oldest and largest grassroots autism organization, founded in 1965 by Dr. Bernard Rimland, Dr. Ruth Sullivan, and a small group of parents. The organization provides education, advocacy, services, and support to the autism community through a national network of local affiliates. The Autism Society believes in the strength of the autism community and promotes acceptance and inclusion of individuals across the entire autism spectrum throughout their life journeys.

sections.title: Local Affiliates and Support
sections.text: The Autism Society's network includes over 70 local affiliates across the United States, providing community-based support and services. Local affiliates offer support groups for autistic individuals and their families, recreational programs, educational workshops, and connections to local resources. Many affiliates organize social events, camps, and activities designed for people on the autism spectrum. Contact your local affiliate to learn about programs available in your community.

sections.title: Information and Resources
sections.text: The Autism Society provides comprehensive information about autism spectrum disorder, including guidance on diagnosis, early intervention, therapies, education, employment, housing, and adult services. The website features articles written by experts and autistic self-advocates, toolkits for families at every stage of the autism journey, and information about evidence-based interventions. Resources are available for newly diagnosed individuals and families, educators, healthcare providers, and employers seeking to support autistic employees.

sections.title: National Helpline
sections.text: The Autism Society's National Helpline provides free information, referrals, and support to anyone seeking assistance. Helpline staff can help connect you with local resources, answer questions about autism, and provide guidance on accessing services. The helpline serves individuals on the autism spectrum, parents, caregivers, educators, and professionals. Contact the helpline through the Autism Society website or by phone to speak with a trained information specialist.

sections.title: Advocacy and Awareness
sections.text: The Autism Society advocates for the needs of the autism community at local, state, and federal levels. Advocacy priorities include insurance coverage for autism services, educational rights, employment opportunities, housing options, and research funding. The organization leads National Autism Awareness Month each April and the Autism Acceptance movement promoting full inclusion of autistic individuals in all aspects of community life. Members can participate in advocacy campaigns, share their stories, and help shape policies affecting the autism community.

sections.title: About Caregiver Action Network
sections.text: Caregiver Action Network (CAN) is a nonprofit organization providing education, peer support, and resources to the more than 53 million Americans who care for loved ones with chronic conditions, disabilities, disease, or the frailties of old age. Founded in 1993, CAN serves as a national voice for family caregivers, working to improve the quality of life for families across the nation. The organization provides free programs and services to help caregivers while they care for their loved ones.

sections.title: Caregiver Help Desk
sections.text: CAN offers a free Caregiver Help Desk where trained staff can answer questions, provide resources, and connect caregivers with services. The Help Desk assists with understanding caregiving basics, finding local resources, navigating healthcare systems, identifying financial assistance programs, and connecting with peer support. Help Desk staff understand the challenges caregivers face and can provide compassionate guidance for a wide range of situations.

sections.title: Educational Programs
sections.text: CAN provides free educational programs covering essential caregiving topics including medication management, communicating with healthcare providers, managing caregiver stress and burnout, understanding disease-specific care needs, financial planning, and legal issues like advance directives. Programs are available online, making them accessible to caregivers who cannot leave home. The organization's Care for the Family Caregiver workshop addresses caregiver self-care and stress management.

sections.title: Peer Support and Community
sections.text: CAN's online Caregiver Community connects family caregivers with others who understand their experiences. Members can share stories, ask questions, and offer support to fellow caregivers in forums organized by topic and care situation. The community provides a safe space to discuss the emotional challenges of caregiving, celebrate small victories, and find solidarity with others facing similar journeys. Peer support helps reduce the isolation that many caregivers experience.

sections.title: Advocacy for Caregivers
sections.text: CAN advocates for public policies that support family caregivers, including paid family leave, workplace flexibility, respite care funding, and caregiver tax credits. The organization works to ensure caregivers' voices are heard in policy discussions at the federal and state levels. CAN's annual National Family Caregivers Month campaign raises awareness about the contributions and needs of family caregivers. Caregivers can participate in advocacy by sharing their stories and contacting legislators.

sections.title: About CHADD
sections.text: CHADD (Children and Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder) is the nation's leading nonprofit organization serving people affected by ADHD. Founded in 1987 by families seeking answers and support, CHADD has grown into a respected resource for accurate, science-based information about ADHD. The organization provides education, advocacy, and support to the millions of children and adults with ADHD, their families, educators, and healthcare professionals. CHADD operates the National Resource Center on ADHD, funded by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

sections.title: Local Chapters and Support Groups
sections.text: CHADD has a network of local chapters and support groups across the United States that provide community-based support and education. Local affiliates host meetings, workshops, and events where people can connect with others who understand ADHD firsthand. Parent support groups help families navigate the challenges of raising a child with ADHD, while adult groups focus on issues like workplace accommodations, relationships, and self-management. Many chapters offer specialized groups for parents, adults with ADHD, and teens.

sections.title: Educational Resources
sections.text: CHADD provides comprehensive, evidence-based information about ADHD through its National Resource Center. Resources cover topics including diagnosis, treatment options, medication, behavioral strategies, school accommodations, and workplace issues. CHADD's website offers fact sheets, webinars, podcasts, and the award-winning Attention magazine. The organization also publishes guides for parents, educators, and healthcare providers. Ask the Expert webinars feature leading ADHD researchers and clinicians sharing the latest knowledge.

sections.title: Training and Educational Programs
sections.text: CHADD offers Parent to Parent, a science-based training program that teaches parents and caregivers skills for managing ADHD behaviors. The ADHD Coaching Certificate Program trains professionals to provide ADHD-specific coaching. Teacher to Teacher provides educators with practical strategies for supporting students with ADHD in the classroom. CHADD's annual international conference brings together thousands of people with ADHD, families, and professionals for workshops, presentations, and networking.

sections.title: Advocacy and Public Policy
sections.text: CHADD advocates at federal and state levels for policies that support people with ADHD. Key advocacy areas include ensuring access to ADHD medications, protecting educational rights under IDEA and Section 504, promoting insurance coverage for ADHD treatment, and increasing research funding. CHADD works to reduce stigma around ADHD and ensure that accurate information reaches the public, policymakers, and media. Members can participate in advocacy campaigns and share their stories to help shape policy.

sections.title: About DBSA
sections.text: The Depression and Bipolar Support Alliance (DBSA) is the leading peer-directed national organization focusing on depression and bipolar disorder. Founded in 1985, DBSA provides hope, help, support, and education to improve the lives of people who have mood disorders. DBSA reaches millions of people each year through its network of nearly 600 peer support groups, educational materials, and online resources. The organization is unique in being led by people who themselves live with mood disorders.

sections.title: Peer Support Groups
sections.text: DBSA operates nearly 600 peer-led support groups across the United States, including both in-person and online options. These groups provide a safe, confidential environment where people can share experiences, coping strategies, and recovery tools. Support groups are free and open to anyone living with depression or bipolar disorder, as well as their family and friends. Group facilitators are trained volunteers who themselves live with mood disorders, creating an atmosphere of genuine understanding and shared experience.

sections.title: Wellness Tools and Resources
sections.text: DBSA offers a comprehensive Wellness Toolbox including mood tracking worksheets, personal wellness plans, and educational resources about mood disorders. The Wellness Wheel helps members identify areas of life that need attention, while the Personal Calendar helps track moods, medications, sleep, and other factors. DBSA's extensive library of brochures and booklets covers topics like understanding depression and bipolar disorder, managing medications, and communicating with healthcare providers.

sections.title: How to Find a Group
sections.text: Visit dbsalliance.org and use the chapter locator to find in-person groups near you. Online support groups meet throughout the week via video conference and are accessible from anywhere. No registration, referral, or formal diagnosis is required—all are welcome. First-time visitors often find it helpful to arrive a few minutes early to meet the facilitator. DBSA also offers a helpline at 1-800-826-3632 where you can learn more about local resources and get questions answered.

sections.title: Advocacy and Research
sections.text: DBSA advocates for improved access to mental health care, insurance parity, and increased research funding for mood disorders. The organization partners with researchers to ensure that the perspectives of people living with mood disorders are included in clinical studies. DBSA's advocacy efforts have contributed to landmark legislation including the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act. Members can participate in advocacy days, share their stories with legislators, and help reduce stigma around mood disorders.

sections.title: About NAMI FaithNet
sections.text: NAMI FaithNet is an interfaith resource network within the National Alliance on Mental Illness that provides resources to faith community leaders, congregations, and individuals who want to address mental health in their faith settings. FaithNet recognizes that for many people, their faith community is a primary source of support, and works to equip faith leaders with the knowledge and tools to support members experiencing mental health challenges. The network serves all faiths and denominations.

sections.title: Resources for Faith Leaders
sections.text: FaithNet provides training and resources for clergy, pastoral counselors, and faith community leaders on recognizing mental health conditions, providing appropriate support, and making referrals to professional care. Resources address how to integrate mental health awareness into sermons, pastoral care, and congregation life. Training helps faith leaders understand when spiritual support is appropriate and when professional mental health treatment is needed, enabling them to guide congregants to appropriate resources.

sections.title: For Congregations
sections.text: FaithNet helps faith communities become welcoming and supportive places for people with mental health conditions and their families. Resources include guides for starting support groups in congregations, mental health awareness materials, and strategies for reducing stigma within faith communities. FaithNet provides toolkits for Mental Health Awareness Sundays and other awareness events that can be adapted for any faith tradition.

sections.title: Bridging Faith and Mental Health
sections.text: Many people struggling with mental health conditions turn first to their faith community before seeking professional help. FaithNet works to ensure these faith communities can provide appropriate, informed support. The network addresses common misconceptions about mental illness in religious contexts—such as beliefs that mental illness results from lack of faith—while honoring the important role that spirituality plays in many people's healing. FaithNet advocates for mental health care that respects and incorporates faith when appropriate.

sections.title: Getting Involved
sections.text: Faith leaders and congregations can access free FaithNet resources through the NAMI website. Resources include downloadable guides, webinars, and connections to local NAMI affiliates that can provide support and training. Individuals whose faith is important to their mental health journey can use FaithNet resources to find faith communities that are welcoming and informed about mental health issues. FaithNet also offers opportunities to share your story and help others understand the intersection of faith and mental health.

sections.title: About the IOCDF
sections.text: The International OCD Foundation (IOCDF) is a nonprofit organization dedicated to helping individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder and related disorders live full and productive lives. The IOCDF works to increase access to effective treatment, promote awareness and understanding of OCD, and support research into the causes and treatments of OCD and related conditions. Founded in 1986, the foundation has become the leading resource for OCD information, treatment, and community support worldwide.

sections.title: OCD Resources
sections.text: The IOCDF provides extensive educational resources about OCD, including information about symptoms, diagnosis, and evidence-based treatments like Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) therapy. The foundation's website offers guides for patients, families, and clinicians, as well as information about related conditions like body dysmorphic disorder and hoarding disorder.

sections.title: Finding Treatment
sections.text: The IOCDF maintains a directory of OCD treatment providers trained in evidence-based approaches. The foundation also provides resources to help you understand treatment options and find specialists in your area. Through local affiliates and online support groups, the IOCDF connects people with OCD to community support.

sections.title: Get Involved
sections.text: Visit iocdf.org to access educational resources, find a treatment provider, or connect with the OCD community. The IOCDF hosts an annual conference bringing together thousands of people affected by OCD, clinicians, and researchers. The foundation also advocates for better insurance coverage and funding for OCD research.

sections.title: About the International OCD Foundation
sections.text: The International OCD Foundation (IOCDF) is a donor-supported nonprofit organization serving the global OCD community. Founded in 1986 by a small group of individuals with OCD, the IOCDF has grown into the leading resource for people affected by OCD and related disorders including body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), hoarding disorder, trichotillomania (hair pulling), and skin picking disorder. The organization's mission is to help everyone affected by OCD and related disorders live full and productive lives.

sections.title: Educational Resources
sections.text: IOCDF provides comprehensive educational materials about OCD and related disorders, including detailed information about symptoms, causes, and evidence-based treatments. Resources cover the distinction between OCD and normal worrying, common OCD subtypes (contamination, harm, religious/scrupulosity, relationship), and guidance for family members. The foundation publishes articles, videos, and guides written and reviewed by leading OCD experts. Their website features first-person stories from people living with OCD who have found effective treatment.

sections.title: Finding OCD Treatment
sections.text: IOCDF maintains a searchable Resource Directory of mental health professionals who specialize in treating OCD using Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), the gold-standard treatment for OCD. You can search for therapists by location, specialty, and treatment approach. The foundation provides guidance on what to look for in an OCD specialist, questions to ask potential providers, and information about intensive treatment programs for severe OCD. They also offer resources about medication options that may complement therapy.

sections.title: Support Groups and Community
sections.text: IOCDF has a network of local affiliates and support groups across the United States and internationally. Support groups provide a space for people with OCD and their family members to share experiences, coping strategies, and encouragement. The foundation hosts the Annual OCD Conference, the largest gathering of OCD community members, researchers, and clinicians in the world. Online communities and forums connect people with OCD year-round, helping reduce the isolation that often accompanies the disorder.

sections.title: Specialized Programs and Initiatives
sections.text: IOCDF runs specialized programs including the Pediatric OCD Program for children, teens, and families; the OCD in the Workplace initiative addressing accommodation and disclosure issues; and the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion initiative to ensure culturally responsive OCD care. The foundation funds research grants to advance understanding and treatment of OCD. Advocacy efforts focus on improving insurance coverage for OCD treatment and increasing access to specialized care across underserved communities.

sections.title: About The JED Foundation
sections.text: The JED Foundation (JED) is a nonprofit organization that partners with teens, young adults, families, high schools, and colleges to strengthen mental health and prevent suicide. Founded in 2000 by Donna and Phil Satow after losing their son Jed to suicide, the organization has become a leading voice in adolescent and young adult mental health. JED works to build emotional resilience and help young people thrive, equipping them with skills and support before crisis occurs.

sections.title: Resources for Teens and Young Adults
sections.text: JED offers extensive free resources for teens and young adults through Set to Go, a comprehensive guide for managing the transition from high school to college or adult life. The website provides practical advice on handling stress, relationships, substance use, and mental health challenges. JED's content addresses common concerns like anxiety, depression, identity exploration, and academic pressure. Resources include videos, articles, self-care tools, and guidance on when and how to seek professional help.

sections.title: JED Campus Program
sections.text: JED Campus is a four-year program that partners with colleges and universities to evaluate and strengthen their mental health, substance misuse, and suicide prevention efforts. Schools work with JED experts to assess current programs, develop strategic plans, and implement evidence-based practices. Over 400 colleges have enrolled in JED Campus, creating safer and more supportive environments for millions of students. The program addresses seven key areas including developing life skills, promoting social connectedness, and following crisis management procedures.

sections.title: High School Programs
sections.text: JED High School extends the organization's expertise to secondary education, helping schools build comprehensive mental health strategies. The program provides assessment tools, resources, and technical assistance to help schools promote emotional well-being, identify students at risk, and respond effectively to mental health crises. JED partners with school administrators, counselors, teachers, and student leaders to create school cultures where mental health is prioritized and students feel comfortable seeking help.

sections.title: Resources for Parents and Families
sections.text: JED provides resources for parents and families to help them support the mental health of young people. Guides cover topics like recognizing warning signs, having conversations about mental health, understanding treatment options, and supporting a young person in crisis. JED's Parent Guide helps families prepare for the emotional challenges of major life transitions. The organization also offers resources specifically for parents who have lost a child to suicide, connecting them with support communities and healing resources.

sections.title: About Latinx Therapy
sections.text: Latinx Therapy is a mental health resource platform created to increase accessibility to culturally competent mental health care for the Latinx community. Founded by Dr. Adriana Alejandre, the organization addresses the significant barriers Latinx individuals face in accessing mental health services, including language barriers, lack of culturally competent providers, and cultural stigma around mental health. Latinx Therapy provides a therapist directory, podcast, and educational resources designed specifically for the Latinx community.

sections.title: Finding a Latinx Therapist
sections.text: The Latinx Therapy directory helps you find mental health professionals who identify as Latinx or specialize in serving Latinx clients. Providers understand cultural factors affecting Latinx mental health including immigration experiences, family dynamics, machismo and marianismo, acculturation stress, and intergenerational trauma. Many providers offer services in Spanish or are bilingual. The directory allows you to search by location, specialty, insurance, and language to find a therapist who can provide culturally responsive care.

sections.title: Latinx Therapy Podcast
sections.text: The Latinx Therapy Podcast is a bilingual podcast that destigmatizes mental health in the Latinx community. Episodes cover topics relevant to Latinx mental health including navigating familia dynamics, immigration trauma, racial identity, dating and relationships, and specific mental health conditions. The podcast features conversations with mental health professionals and community members, making mental health information accessible in a familiar, culturally relevant format. Episodes are available in both English and Spanish.

sections.title: Culturally Relevant Resources
sections.text: Latinx Therapy provides articles, guides, and resources that address mental health through a cultural lens. Resources acknowledge the unique stressors facing Latinx communities including discrimination, immigration concerns, language barriers, and the pressure to support extended family. Educational content helps community members understand mental health conditions, recognize when to seek help, and communicate about mental health with family members who may hold different beliefs. Resources emphasize that seeking help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

sections.title: Community and Impact
sections.text: Latinx Therapy works to change how the Latinx community views and accesses mental health care. The organization partners with community groups, universities, and media outlets to spread mental health awareness and reduce stigma. By providing free accessible resources and amplifying Latinx voices in mental health, Latinx Therapy helps ensure that cultural background is not a barrier to getting help. The organization's vision is a Latinx community where mental health is prioritized and culturally competent care is accessible to all.

sections.title: About Muslim Mental Health Services
sections.text: Sanctuary for Families provides culturally sensitive mental health services designed specifically for Muslim individuals and families. Understanding the unique cultural and religious factors that affect Muslim mental health, these services offer support that respects Islamic values while providing evidence-based care. The program addresses barriers many Muslims face in accessing mental health care, including stigma within the community, concerns about providers understanding Islamic beliefs, and lack of culturally competent services.

sections.title: Mental Health Services
sections.text: Services include individual therapy, family counseling, support groups, and crisis intervention provided by clinicians who understand Muslim culture and can integrate clients' faith into treatment when appropriate. Therapists are trained to work with issues common in Muslim communities including intergenerational conflict, cultural identity, discrimination and Islamophobia, immigration stress, and family dynamics. Services can be provided in multiple languages and accommodate religious observances.

sections.title: Culturally Informed Approach
sections.text: Providers understand the role of faith, family, and community in Muslim life and can work within these frameworks rather than against them. The approach recognizes that for many Muslims, mental health and spiritual health are interconnected, and treatment should honor this connection. Clinicians understand concepts like family honor, gender dynamics in traditional families, and the importance of community reputation while helping clients navigate their individual mental health needs.

sections.title: Addressing Stigma
sections.text: Many Muslim communities have historically stigmatized mental health issues, viewing them as a lack of faith or something to be handled privately within the family. These services help bridge this gap by providing education about mental health from a culturally informed perspective, showing how seeking help aligns with Islamic values of self-care and betterment, and creating safe spaces where Muslims can address mental health without judgment from within or outside their community.

sections.title: Getting Help
sections.text: If you're a Muslim individual or family member seeking culturally competent mental health support, these services provide a safe and understanding environment. Services may be available on a sliding scale or free depending on circumstances. Contact the program to learn about available services, hours, and how to schedule an appointment. You deserve mental health support that understands and respects your faith and culture.

sections.title: About Family-to-Family
sections.text: NAMI Family-to-Family is a free, 8-session educational program for family members, significant others, and friends of people living with mental health conditions. The program is taught by trained family members who have firsthand experience supporting loved ones with mental illness. It provides education about mental health conditions, treatment approaches, and evidence-based communication strategies.

sections.title: What You'll Learn
sections.text: The Family-to-Family curriculum covers understanding major mental health conditions including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, anxiety disorders, and others. Participants learn about treatment options including medications and therapy, how to handle crises, effective communication and problem-solving skills, advocacy strategies, and self-care for caregivers.

sections.title: How the Program Works
sections.text: Family-to-Family classes meet weekly for 8 sessions, each lasting about 2-2.5 hours. Classes are offered in-person and online through local NAMI affiliates across the United States. The small group format allows participants to share experiences and support each other while learning from trained peer instructors who understand the caregiving journey.

sections.title: How to Enroll
sections.text: Family-to-Family is completely free. To find a class near you, visit nami.org or contact your local NAMI affiliate. Classes fill up quickly, so early registration is recommended. Participants should be family members or friends of someone with a mental health condition. The program has helped hundreds of thousands of families since its creation.

sections.title: About Narcotics Anonymous
sections.text: Narcotics Anonymous (NA) is a global, community-based organization with a multilingual and multicultural membership. Founded in 1953, NA offers recovery from the effects of addiction through working a twelve-step program including regular attendance at group meetings. The only requirement for membership is a desire to stop using drugs. NA makes no distinction between drugs including alcohol—the focus is on addiction as a disease that affects every area of life. NA is not affiliated with any treatment centers, religions, political organizations, or institutions.

sections.title: How NA Works
sections.text: NA is a program of complete abstinence from all drugs. The Twelve Steps of NA provide a framework for personal recovery that addresses the physical, mental, and spiritual aspects of addiction. Members work through these steps with the support of a sponsor—an experienced member who has worked the steps themselves. Regular meeting attendance, phone contact with other members, and service work are key components. NA emphasizes that addiction is a disease, not a moral failing, and that recovery is possible through mutual support and spiritual growth.

sections.title: Finding NA Meetings
sections.text: NA has more than 70,000 weekly meetings in 144 countries worldwide. Meetings are held in-person at various community locations and online through virtual meeting platforms. Visit na.org and use the meeting search tool to find meetings near you. Meeting formats include open meetings (anyone can attend), closed meetings (for addicts only), speaker meetings, discussion meetings, step study, and tradition study groups. Most areas have meetings available every day of the week, often multiple times per day.

sections.title: What to Expect at Your First Meeting
sections.text: NA meetings are welcoming to newcomers. Meetings typically open with readings from NA literature, followed by sharing from members or a speaker. You are never required to speak, introduce yourself, or share anything personal. What you hear at meetings is confidential. Many meetings have a newcomer's welcome where first-time visitors can ask questions. You may be offered phone numbers from members willing to talk between meetings. There are no dues or fees—NA is entirely self-supporting through member contributions.

sections.title: Getting Started in NA
sections.text: If you think you may have a problem with drugs, NA suggests attending several meetings to get a feel for the program. Each meeting has its own atmosphere, so trying different groups can help you find where you feel comfortable. Consider getting a sponsor—someone to guide you through the steps and answer questions. NA literature, including the Basic Text and informational pamphlets, provides detailed information about the program. Many areas have helplines staffed by NA members who can answer questions and provide meeting information. The NA website also offers online resources and virtual meetings.

sections.title: About NEDA
sections.text: The National Eating Disorders Association (NEDA) is the largest nonprofit organization dedicated to supporting individuals and families affected by eating disorders. NEDA serves as a catalyst for prevention, cures, and access to quality care. The organization provides education, resources, and support while advocating for research and policies that increase understanding and improve treatment for eating disorders including anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, and ARFID.

sections.title: NEDA Helpline and Support
sections.text: NEDA offers support through multiple channels. For crisis situations involving eating disorders, text NEDA to 741741 to connect with a trained Crisis Text Line counselor. The NEDA website provides a chat feature for non-crisis support and information. Helpline services can assist with finding treatment providers, understanding insurance coverage, locating support groups, and providing information about eating disorders. All services are free and confidential, staffed by trained volunteers who understand eating disorders.

sections.title: Screening and Assessment Tools
sections.text: NEDA provides free, confidential screening tools on their website to help individuals determine if they or a loved one may be struggling with an eating disorder. These evidence-based questionnaires cover symptoms of various eating disorders and disordered eating patterns. While screenings cannot provide a diagnosis, they can help identify warning signs and encourage people to seek professional evaluation. NEDA also offers resources for healthcare providers on recognizing and screening for eating disorders in clinical settings.

sections.title: Finding Treatment
sections.text: NEDA maintains a treatment provider directory that helps individuals find eating disorder specialists, treatment centers, and programs across the United States. The website provides guidance on different levels of care, from outpatient treatment to residential programs. NEDA offers information on navigating insurance coverage for eating disorder treatment, appealing denials, and understanding patients' rights. Resources include questions to ask treatment providers and information about evidence-based treatments for different types of eating disorders.

sections.title: Community and Support Groups
sections.text: NEDA facilitates peer support through online forums, virtual support groups, and connections to local resources. NEDA Walks bring together communities across the country to raise awareness and support for eating disorder prevention and recovery. The organization also provides resources specifically for parents, partners, and families supporting a loved one with an eating disorder, including guidance on communication, meal support, and self-care for caregivers. NEDA's National Eating Disorders Awareness Week each February provides opportunities for community education and advocacy.

sections.title: About PSI
sections.text: Postpartum Support International (PSI) is a nonprofit dedicated to helping families experiencing perinatal mental health conditions including postpartum depression, anxiety, OCD, psychosis, and PTSD. Founded in 1987, PSI ensures no family faces perinatal mental health challenges alone. The organization provides peer support, professional training, and advocacy for improved awareness and treatment worldwide.

sections.title: Support Services
sections.text: PSI's helpline at 1-800-944-4773 connects callers with trained volunteers who have personal experience with perinatal mental health conditions. Messages receive callbacks within 24-48 hours. Weekly online support groups meet via video conference in English and Spanish, with specialized groups for fathers and partners. PSI's network of volunteer state and international coordinators can connect families with local resources and providers.

sections.title: Conditions and Treatment
sections.text: PSI addresses all perinatal mood and anxiety disorders affecting anyone during pregnancy or postpartum—including fathers and adoptive parents. These treatable conditions include postpartum depression, postpartum anxiety, postpartum OCD, postpartum psychosis, and postpartum PTSD. PSI maintains a provider directory of perinatal mental health specialists and offers professional training certification for clinicians.

sections.title: Educational Resources
sections.text: PSI's website offers comprehensive information about perinatal mental health conditions, screening tools, and treatment approaches. Resources include guides for family members, materials for healthcare providers on screening and diagnosis, and information about evidence-based treatments. PSI hosts an annual conference bringing together researchers, clinicians, and advocates to advance perinatal mental health care.

sections.title: Climb Out of the Darkness
sections.text: PSI's annual Climb Out of the Darkness event is the world's largest event raising awareness of perinatal mental health. Thousands of families participate in climbs, walks, and virtual events worldwide, helping to reduce stigma and connect those affected by perinatal mood disorders. The event raises funds to support PSI's free programs and services while building community among survivors, families, and advocates working to improve perinatal mental health care.

sections.title: Getting Help
sections.text: If you or someone you know is struggling during pregnancy or postpartum, help is available. Call the PSI helpline at 1-800-944-4773, text 503-894-9453 in English, or text 971-203-7773 in Spanish. You'll receive a callback from a trained volunteer who understands what you're going through. PSI can connect you with local support groups, therapists who specialize in perinatal mental health, and other resources. Remember: you are not alone, you are not to blame, and with help, you will be well.

sections.title: About S&PA Alliance
sections.text: The Schizophrenia & Psychosis Action Alliance (S&PA, formerly Schizophrenia and Related Disorders Alliance of America) is the only national nonprofit focused exclusively on improving the lives of people affected by schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders. Founded in 2009, S&PA provides peer support, education, and advocacy for individuals living with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and psychosis, as well as their families. The organization emphasizes the importance of lived experience in shaping programs and policies.

sections.title: Support and Connection
sections.text: S&PA offers peer support groups where people living with schizophrenia and psychosis can connect with others who understand their experiences. Online support groups meet regularly via video conference, providing a safe space for sharing, encouragement, and practical coping strategies. The organization also provides family support resources, recognizing that psychotic disorders affect entire families. Connection with peers who have achieved stability and recovery provides hope and practical guidance.

sections.title: Education and Resources
sections.text: S&PA provides educational resources about schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and other psychotic conditions. Materials cover topics including understanding symptoms, treatment options, medication management, navigating the mental health system, and recovery strategies. The organization offers webinars featuring experts and people with lived experience. Resources emphasize that recovery is possible—many people with schizophrenia lead fulfilling lives with proper treatment and support.

sections.title: Advocacy Efforts
sections.text: S&PA advocates for improved treatment, services, and policies affecting people with serious mental illness. Advocacy priorities include increasing access to evidence-based treatments like Coordinated Specialty Care for first-episode psychosis, improving community mental health services, reforming involuntary treatment laws, and ensuring housing and employment opportunities for people with psychotic disorders. The organization works to reduce stigma by amplifying the voices of people living successfully with these conditions.

sections.title: Getting Involved
sections.text: People affected by schizophrenia and psychosis can join support groups, share their stories, participate in advocacy efforts, and connect with a community that understands. S&PA welcomes individuals living with psychotic disorders, family members, mental health professionals, and allies. The organization's annual conference brings together advocates, clinicians, and researchers. By joining S&PA, you can help change the conversation about schizophrenia and ensure that people with these conditions receive the support and opportunities they deserve.

sections.title: About SMART Recovery
sections.text: SMART Recovery (Self-Management and Recovery Training) is a global community of mutual-support groups that help people recover from all types of addiction and addictive behaviors. Unlike 12-step programs, SMART Recovery is a science-based approach grounded in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT). The program teaches practical skills for building motivation, coping with urges, managing thoughts and behaviors, and living a balanced life. SMART Recovery is secular and does not require belief in a higher power.

sections.title: The Four-Point Program
sections.text: SMART Recovery's approach centers on four key points: Building and maintaining motivation to change; Coping with urges to use; Managing thoughts, feelings, and behaviors; and Living a balanced life. Each point includes specific tools and techniques that participants learn and practice. The program emphasizes self-empowerment and developing internal resources rather than relying on external support indefinitely. Participants learn to identify and dispute irrational beliefs that contribute to addictive behavior and replace them with healthier thinking patterns.

sections.title: Types of Meetings and Support
sections.text: SMART Recovery offers multiple ways to participate: in-person meetings held at community locations nationwide and worldwide, online meetings via video conference, and 24/7 online message board communities. Meetings are typically 90 minutes and are led by trained volunteer facilitators. Unlike some programs, SMART Recovery welcomes cross-talk and discussion during meetings. Specialized meetings are available for specific populations including family and friends of those with addiction, teens, and people in the criminal justice system.

sections.title: Getting Started with SMART Recovery
sections.text: Anyone struggling with addiction can attend SMART Recovery meetings free of charge. Visit smartrecovery.org to find meetings near you or join an online meeting from anywhere. The website offers free resources including the SMART Recovery Handbook, toolbox exercises, and educational videos. New participants are encouraged to attend several meetings to learn the program's tools and techniques. Unlike some recovery programs, SMART does not require lifelong attendance—members are encouraged to graduate when they feel ready to manage their recovery independently.

sections.title: SMART Recovery Family & Friends
sections.text: SMART Recovery offers a dedicated program for family members and friends affected by a loved one's addiction. The Family & Friends program teaches the CRAFT (Community Reinforcement and Family Training) approach, an evidence-based method that helps families improve communication, set boundaries, encourage treatment-seeking, and take care of their own well-being. Family meetings provide support and practical skills, regardless of whether the person with addiction is in recovery. Like the main program, Family & Friends is free, confidential, and available both in-person and online.
